text:
Delta, Georgia Leaders Unite to Accelerate Sustainable Aviation Fuel Growth

(Delta News Hub) The Georgia Sustainable Aviation Fuel Coalition aims to leverage the state's strengths in aviation, agriculture, forestry, research and logistics to help accelerate sustainable aviation fuel development and production.

Delta Air Lines joined partners across Georgia to launch the Georgia Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) Coalition, a new statewide effort established by the Metro Atlanta Chamber and founding members Delta, the Georgia Forestry Association and Georgia Farm Bureau. The coalition aims to advance SAF production and drive economic investment across Georgia. SAF is an alternative jet fuel made from renewable feedstocks that can significantly reduce lifecycle carbon emissions compared to conventional jet fuel.

During an event at the Delta Flight Museum, elected officials, industry leaders and coalition partners gathered to highlight Georgia's opportunity to become a leader in sustainable aviation fuel production. Speakers included Georgia House Speaker Jon Burns, Georgia Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper, Metro Atlanta Chamber President and CEO Katie Kirkpatrick and Delta President Peter Carter.

"Georgia is well positioned to become a national leader in SAF," said Peter Carter, President of Delta Air Lines. "The Georgia SAF Coalition unites organizations committed to advancing that opportunity. Together, we can power the growth of a SAF industry that strengthens Georgia’s economy, supports innovation and creates lasting benefits for communities across the state.”

The coalition builds on momentum created by this year's Keep Georgia Forested Act, legislation that encourages investment in forestry manufacturing and creates new opportunities to convert Georgia-grown agricultural and forestry feedstocks into products such as sustainable aviation fuel.

Priorities include strengthening public-private partnerships, supporting research and commercialization, attracting investment, advancing policies that support industry growth and connecting Georgia's existing strengths to emerging opportunities.

As home to Delta's global headquarters and the world's busiest airport, Georgia is already helping shape the future of aviation. Combined with the nation's largest forestry resource base, strong agricultural production, leading research institutions and a robust logistics network, the state is uniquely positioned to build a sustainable aviation fuel ecosystem that supports farmers, foresters and local communities while creating new economic opportunities across Georgia.

SAF is widely viewed as one of the most promising tools available today to reduce lifecycle carbon emissions from air travel, and Georgia has the feedstock resources, research capabilities and business leadership needed to help scale the industry.

text:
Boeing has identified a potential software glitch in the 737 MAX that can cause the automated flight navigation system to disable during a failed landing attempt, according to a report from the Wall Street Journal (WSJ). This issue has raised concerns over increased pilot workload during a critical phase of flight and prompted a review by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

What’s the issue?

After a recent software update, the aircraft’s automated vertical navigation system (VNAV) could disengage if a pilot changes the pre-programmed flight path in the Flight Management Computer (FMC) following a missed approach or go-around. Although the autopilot remains engaged, pilots would need to input manual vertical and pitch controls, which could pose safety concerns, particularly at low-altitude airports.

The Response

Boeing issued an industry-wide fleet notice in August 2026 to all Boeing 737 MAX operators informing them of the glitch, stating that they do not consider the issue a safety risk and autopilot would remain functional. According to the WSJ, Boeing has plans to provide further clarification in November 2026 and a software patch in early 2028.

The company first became aware of the problem in November 2024, but at the time it was not deemed to meet standards for a safety review. Following subsequent correspondence with 737 MAX operators and a formal safety review this month, Boeing passed the information onto aircraft operators and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

Southwest Airlines and United Airlines have informed Boeing of their intentions to avoid the new software and instead use previous versions. Several airlines including Alaska, American, Southwest and United have confirmed that they are not currently operating the new software in their 737 MAX fleet.

The Boeing 737 MAX family has previously faced intense scrutiny following two fatal crashes in October 2018 and March 2019, linked to the Maneuvering Characteristics Augmentation System (MCAS).

The FAA & the MAX 10

There are currently around 2,400 737 MAX 8 and 9 aircraft in operation. The FAA has since delayed certification of the Boeing 737 MAX 10, the largest of the MAX family, until a full safety risk assessment has been established. On Oct. 2, 2026, the aviation authority convened a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) to assess the safety concerns around the software glitch.

The FAA has determined that the software glitch does not pose a safety risk, as pilots retain full control of the aircraft and indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous.

A Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin (SAIB) will be issued to U.S. airlines and foreign regulators.

title: Chile Joins Brazil and Other Places in Coping with Skyrocketing Airfare Surge Due to Jet ...
description:

Impact on Brazilian Consumers: Analysing Ticket Price Data The direct consequence of these soaring costs is a pronounced skyrocketing airfare surge that affects everyday travellers.
In a bid to counter the skyrocketing airfare surge, nations moved towards deep integration and the liberalisation of their airspace.

If the US dollar maintains its strength against Latin American currencies, the financial pressure on carriers in Brazil, Chile, and neighbouring nations will persist unabated.
text:
The Latin American aviation sector is facing an unprecedented financial paradox in late 2026. While passenger numbers are shattering historical records across the continent, airlines are grappling with a severe operational crisis. The relentless escalation of aviation fuel costs, driven by international conflicts and global supply chain disruptions, has triggered a massive skyrocketing airfare surge that is directly impacting millions of travellers. With industry profitability plummeting and fuel expenses eating into nearly half of all operational budgets, nations like Brazil and Chile are urgently seeking structural solutions. This article explores how governments, airlines, and passengers are navigating this challenging turbulence.

The Macroeconomic Context: An Unforeseen Aviation Crisis in 2026

The global aviation industry entered 2026 with an atmosphere of profound optimism. Following years of post-pandemic recovery, international and domestic travel demand had stabilised, and airlines were aggressively expanding their route networks. However, the macroeconomic realities of late 2026 have painted a drastically different picture. The commercial aviation landscape is now defined by a crippling skyrocketing airfare surge, fundamentally driven by volatile energy markets.

The primary catalyst for this economic turbulence is the sustained elevation of jet fuel prices. Geopolitical tensions, particularly the renewed and intense conflicts in the Middle East, have sent shockwaves through the global petroleum supply chain. For nations in Latin America, such as Brazil and Chile, these international shocks are magnified by local currency fluctuations, complex taxation systems, and logistical constraints. Despite airlines operating flights at near-maximum capacity, the staggering cost of fuel has completely eroded profit margins, forcing carriers to pass the financial burden onto consumers. This complex interplay between record-breaking consumer demand and historically high operational costs forms the crux of the current crisis affecting the continent.

Global Jet Fuel Pricing Dynamics: IATA’s Grim 2026 Forecast

To fully understand the severity of the skyrocketing airfare surge, one must examine the baseline data provided by international regulatory and monitoring bodies. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) issued a highly sobering report in mid-2026, drastically revising its annual projections for the industry. According to IATA’s official figures, global jet fuel prices are expected to average a staggering USD 152 per barrel throughout 2026.

This figure represents a dramatic increase of nearly 70 per cent compared to the average prices recorded in 2025. The exponential rise in Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) costs has triggered an immediate and severe contraction in airline profitability. IATA was forced to halve its 2026 global airline profit forecast, downgrading expectations from an initially projected USD 41 billion down to a mere USD 23 billion. For an industry that operates on notoriously thin margins, a 70 per cent year-on-year increase in its largest single expense category is nothing short of catastrophic.

In Latin America, the situation is particularly acute. Unlike major carriers in North America or Europe, which often benefit from extensive fuel hedging programmes and robust local currencies, Latin American airlines are highly exposed to the US dollar. Because aviation fuel is priced globally in dollars, the depreciation of regional currencies against the greenback has created a devastating multiplier effect on operational expenditures.

Brazil’s Aviation Sector: Record Demand Meets Escalating Operational Pressures

Brazil, the largest aviation market in Latin America, serves as a prime case study for the current crisis. The National Civil Aviation Agency (ANAC) recently published highly detailed statistics showcasing a booming domestic market. Between January and August 2026, Brazil recorded an impressive 68.3 million passengers on domestic flights. August 2026 alone set a new historical record for domestic air travel, with 8.93 million passengers flying within the country—a 2.3 per cent increase compared to the 8.73 million passengers recorded in August 2025.

However, this robust demand is masking severe underlying financial distress. The skyrocketing airfare surge in Brazil is a direct mathematical consequence of the pricing policies applied to Querosene de Aviação (QAV), the local terminology for jet fuel. Data from ANAC and the Brazilian Association of Airlines (Abear) reveals a startling trajectory. In June 2026, QAV was priced at R$ 5.66 per litre, which already represented a 57.6 per cent increase compared to June 2025.

The Petrobras Factor and the October 2026 Price Hike

The situation deteriorated further as the year progressed. By October 2026, Petrobras, the state-owned multinational energy corporation, announced another severe readjustment. Citing renewed geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and international market fluctuations, Petrobras implemented an 11.8 per cent hike in the sale price of fuel to distributors.

According to Abear’s industry calculations, this pushed the refinery price of QAV past the R$ 6.28 per litre mark. To contextualise the sheer velocity of this inflation, the reference price for a litre of QAV was just R$ 3.31 in February 2026. This represents an approximate 90 per cent increase in a span of just eight months.

For Brazilian airlines, fuel is no longer just a major expense; it is an existential threat. Abear officially confirmed that QAV now accounts for approximately 46 per cent of the total operational expenses for airlines operating in Brazil. Furthermore, the association reported that the sector has already spent an unanticipated R$ 7.6 billion extra on fuel in 2026, far exceeding the projections made prior to the global oil shocks.

Impact on Brazilian Consumers: Analysing Ticket Price Data

The direct consequence of these soaring costs is a pronounced skyrocketing airfare surge that affects everyday travellers. Official data released by ANAC highlighted that the average domestic airfare in June 2026 stood at R$ 660.54 per segment. While nearly 47.2 per cent of seats sold that month remained under the R$ 500 threshold, a growing percentage of tickets (6.3 per cent) were sold for values exceeding R$ 1,500.

Industry experts and government officials warn that if QAV prices continue their upward trajectory, the fundamental connectivity of the nation is at risk. Brazil is a continent-sized country where air travel is not a luxury, but a necessity for business, healthcare access, and regional integration. The persistent cost pressures threaten to reverse years of democratisation in Brazilian air travel, potentially forcing airlines to abandon less profitable regional routes in favour of highly concentrated, lucrative trunk routes between major economic hubs like São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, and Brasília.

Chile’s Resilience: Shattering Passenger Records Amidst Rising Fares

While Brazil struggles with domestic fuel pricing, its neighbour Chile faces a similar yet distinct set of challenges. The Chilean aviation market, heavily reliant on both robust domestic networks and strategic international connections, has also witnessed unprecedented travel demand in 2026.

Official figures released by the Junta de Aeronáutica Civil (JAC) and airport authorities illustrate this boom. Santiago de Chile Airport (Arturo Merino Benítez International Airport) surpassed a monumental milestone by welcoming 13,087,297 passengers in the first half of 2026 alone. This surge builds upon the momentum of the previous year, where the Chilean air transport sector reached an all-time historical record of over 28.2 million passengers, reflecting a robust 13 per cent year-on-year growth.

Despite these overwhelmingly positive traffic figures, Chilean carriers are deeply exposed to the same international fuel market volatilities identified by IATA. Chile imports the vast majority of its refined petroleum products, making its aviation sector highly vulnerable to global supply shocks. Consequently, Chilean consumers are increasingly subjected to a skyrocketing airfare surge, particularly on international long-haul routes and domestic flights traversing the extensive length of the country, from Arica in the north to Punta Arenas in the deep south.

The Chilean Government’s Proactive Response

Unlike markets that have adopted a purely reactive stance, the Chilean government, operating through the JAC and the Ministry of Transport and Telecommunications, has taken proactive regulatory steps to mitigate the crisis and ensure long-term sustainability. The strategy has been twofold: aggressively expanding international bilateral agreements to foster competition, and heavily investing in the research and implementation of Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF).

The Cross-Border Solution: Historic Open Skies Agreements

Recognising that protectionist policies only exacerbate pricing pressures during energy crises, Latin American governments executed a historic regulatory shift in mid-2026. In a bid to counter the skyrocketing airfare surge, nations moved towards deep integration and the liberalisation of their airspace.

On 14 July 2026, in Asunción, the aeronautical authorities of Chile, Argentina, Brazil, and Paraguay signed a landmark Liberalisation Agreement. This monumental treaty paved the way for unprecedented cross-border operational freedom. Shortly thereafter, on 22 July 2026, Chile and Brazil officially formalised an amendment to their Route Framework, agreeing to the total opening of their passenger air services.

This “Open Skies” policy is a critical macroeconomic tool. By allowing airlines from participating nations to operate freely across borders without traditional frequency or capacity restrictions, governments aim to stimulate intense market competition. In theory, increased competition should exert downward pressure on ticket prices, helping to offset the debilitating costs of jet fuel. It also allows airlines to optimise their fleet utilisation across a broader regional network, thereby improving operational efficiency in a high-cost environment.

Economic Implications: Inflation, Trade, and Tourism Repercussions

The repercussions of the skyrocketing airfare surge extend far beyond the immediate balance sheets of commercial airlines; they possess the capacity to disrupt broader national economies. In both Brazil and Chile, air transportation is a critical economic enabler, underpinning the tourism industry, facilitating corporate commerce, and driving time-sensitive cargo logistics.

The Tourism Sector Impact

The tourism industry is arguably the most vulnerable to sustained hikes in airfares. In Brazil, destinations in the Northeast (Nordeste)—which rely heavily on domestic tourists travelling from the affluent Southern and Southeastern states—face the prospect of decreased visitor numbers if flights become prohibitively expensive. Similarly, in Chile, remote and highly sought-after tourist destinations such as the Atacama Desert, Easter Island, and the Patagonian fjords depend almost entirely on affordable air connectivity.

When airfares surge, the total cost of a holiday package inflates, forcing consumers to either downgrade their accommodation choices, reduce their length of stay, or cancel their travel plans entirely. This creates a cascading economic effect that harms local hoteliers, restaurateurs, and regional tour operators whose livelihoods are inextricably linked to a steady flow of airborne tourists.

Corporate Travel and Cargo Logistics

The corporate travel sector is also feeling the strain. While large multinational corporations may absorb higher ticket prices, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are being forced to curtail business travel, replacing face-to-face meetings with virtual alternatives. This reduction in corporate mobility can subtly hinder regional trade negotiations and business expansion efforts.

Furthermore, air cargo—which relies heavily on belly-hold capacity in passenger aircraft—is experiencing parallel cost inflation. High-value exports, such as Chilean salmon and Brazilian pharmaceuticals, are subjected to increased freight tariffs, thereby reducing their competitiveness in the global market.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF): The Long-Term Escape Route

While Open Skies agreements provide a vital regulatory mechanism to foster competition, they do not solve the fundamental problem of reliance on expensive, price-volatile fossil fuels. Acknowledging this reality, Latin American governments have accelerated their transition towards Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF) as the definitive long-term solution to prevent future instances of the skyrocketing airfare surge.

Chile has emerged as a regional pioneer in this environmental and economic transition. Through its “Vuelo Limpio” (Clean Flight) programme, operating in conjunction with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), Chile has aggressively pursued SAF feasibility. On 7 July 2026, the Chilean government presented a landmark study on the potential of Used Cooking Oils (UCO) for SAF production—a critical milestone for the decarbonisation of the nation’s air transport. Later in October 2026, ICAO officially published a comprehensive Feasibility Study on the Use of Sustainable Aviation Fuels in Chile.

Brazil, possessing one of the world’s most advanced agricultural sectors and a massive existing biofuel industry (ethanol and biodiesel), is uniquely positioned to become a global superpower in SAF production. The bilateral cooperation between the two nations was cemented during Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s state visit to Chile, where a strategic agreement was signed specifically to promote the joint development and commercialisation of Sustainable Aviation Fuels.

By developing a robust, localised SAF supply chain, South American nations can insulate their aviation sectors from the geopolitical shocks of the Middle East and the volatility of the US dollar. Although SAF currently remains more expensive to produce than traditional QAV, the economies of scale, coupled with aggressive government mandates and subsidies, are expected to achieve price parity in the coming decade.

Industry Strategic Shifts: How Airlines Are Surviving 2026

Faced with IATA’s grim profit forecasts and Petrobras’s relentless price hikes, Latin American airlines are deploying a variety of survival strategies. The focus has shifted from aggressive market share acquisition to rigorous margin protection.

Firstly, carriers are executing severe capacity discipline. Airlines are meticulously analysing route profitability, swiftly cutting underperforming regional routes, and consolidating flights to maintain higher load factors. Flying a half-empty aircraft in a market where fuel dictates 46 per cent of costs is an unsustainable luxury.

Secondly, there is an accelerated push towards fleet modernisation. Airlines are phasing out older, less fuel-efficient aircraft in favour of next-generation jets that offer 15 to 25 per cent better fuel economy. While this requires significant capital expenditure in the short term, it provides a crucial structural defence against the skyrocketing airfare surge.

Lastly, ancillary revenue models are being aggressively expanded. To keep base fares ostensibly competitive, airlines are unbundling services, charging premium fees for baggage, seat selection, priority boarding, and in-flight catering. This strategy allows carriers to offset fuel costs without immediately raising the headline ticket price to psychologically prohibitive levels.

Future Outlook: Stabilisation or Prolonged Turbulence in 2027?

As 2026 draws to a close, the million-dollar question for consumers and industry stakeholders is whether the skyrocketing airfare surge will abate in 2027. The outlook remains cautiously complex.

On the pessimistic side, as long as geopolitical instability persists in major oil-producing regions, the baseline cost of crude oil—and by extension, jet fuel—will remain highly elevated and volatile. If the US dollar maintains its strength against Latin American currencies, the financial pressure on carriers in Brazil, Chile, and neighbouring nations will persist unabated.

Conversely, there are glimmers of hope. The implementation of the July 2026 Open Skies agreements will likely mature by early 2027, introducing new competitive dynamics that could help suppress runaway ticket prices. Furthermore, the relentless push towards SAF infrastructure signals a structural shift that will eventually yield energy independence for the region’s aviation sector.

For the immediate future, however, travellers must adapt to a new normal. The era of ultra-cheap, highly subsidised air travel may be temporarily suspended. Consumers will need to employ strategic booking practices—purchasing tickets well in advance, utilising frequent flyer miles, and remaining flexible with travel dates—to navigate the financial turbulence.

In summary, the aviation crisis of late 2026 serves as a harsh reminder of the industry’s vulnerability to macroeconomic and geopolitical forces. The combined efforts of the Brazilian and Chilean governments, through regulatory liberalisation and sustainability initiatives, provide a robust blueprint for recovery. Yet, until the global energy markets achieve a degree of sustainable equilibrium, the Latin American skies will remain an economically challenging airspace to navigate.

text:
This story was first published on RealAgriculture.com on Sept. 30, 2026.

As record-high fuel costs mount during harvest, the Conservative Party is proposing an ‘Emergency Fuel Relief Plan’ to lower diesel prices.

However, Pierre Poilievre’s plan to slash diesel costs comes with a trade-off that could reduce domestic demand for oilseeds — especially canola — as a growing portion of the crop flows into the North American market for renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel.

Read more:

Diesel prices in Canada hitting a record high this harvest

Warm weather helps Sask. farmers make solid progress on 2026 harvest

Farm groups call for national plant breeding strategy and renewed investment

Poilievre and other Conservative MPs, including John Barlow, Shadow Minister for Agriculture and Agri-Food, have pitched a series of short- and longer-term fixes to address the diesel price spike, which they note has led to daily fuel bills for a single combine this fall exceeding $1,100.

To provide quick cost relief, the Conservatives are calling on the Liberal government to:

Eliminate the GST on fuel sales and extend the federal excise tax cut through July 1, 2027.

Scrap the industrial carbon tax and the Clean Fuel Standard (officially known as the Clean Fuel Regulations, or CFR) to lower production costs for refiners. Poilievre has previously referred to the CFR as the “second carbon tax.”

While immediate tax relief on fuel is an easy sell, scrapping renewable fuel requirements could come with consequences for the oilseed market.

Renewable fuel mandates in Canada and the U.S. have been a primary driver behind the multibillion-dollar wave of investment in Prairie canola processing over the last several years, including a major expansion in Western Canadian canola- crushing capacity and Imperial Oil’s renewable diesel facility near Edmonton.

According to the Canadian Canola Growers Association and Canadian Oilseed Processors Association, approximately one out of three acres of canola grown in Western Canada now flows into the North American fuel market, building domestic demand for millions of tonnes of seed while reducing exposure to foreign trade barriers.

The Carney government consulted on amendments to the CFR earlier this year after making a commitment in September 2025 to update the regulations to support domestic biofuel production. Industry sources say they expect the government will publish its proposed amendments in the coming weeks, if not days. On the ethanol side, Canadian producers are calling for changes to level the playing field with American imports, as they are struggling to compete with ethanol subsidized by the 45Z tax break in the U.S.

Regarding fuel taxes, the federal government did extend its federal fuel excise tax cut in early September —10 cents per litre off gasoline and 4 cents per litre off diesel — through Jan. 31, 2027.

Provincially, Alberta and Prince Edward Island have also enacted fuel tax relief, with the Alberta government reducing its 13- cent-per-litre tax on clear gasoline and clear diesel to zero as of October 1.

In the longer term, Poilievre and the Conservatives say the government should expand domestic refining and distribution to hit one million barrels per day of Canadian-refined fuel within five years, which they say would shrink the 32-cent-per-litre price premium Canadians currently pay compared to American diesel users.

To get there, the party is proposing pre-approved environmental and safety permitting for refineries and pipelines, a 100-per-cent year-one tax write-off for capital investments in fuel infrastructure, and the creation of a national Strategic Petroleum Reserve contracted through domestic refiners.

text:
Con la diversificazione e gli stoccaggi di gas, la raffinazione italiana è un pezzo importante della sicurezza energetica del Paese. Oggi l’Italia dispone ancora di una capacità di raffinazione di circa 83 milioni di tonnellate l’anno, distribuita fra dieci raffinerie tradizionali. Nel 2025 sono stati lavorati circa 64 milioni di prodotti: un livello di utilizzo intorno al 77%. Dietro questi numeri si rivela un’industria molto ridimensionata rispetto a quella degli anni Novanta quando le raffinerie erano 20 e la capacità era intorno ai 100 milioni di tonnellate. Ma anche un’industria a “mezzo” servizio. Sotto la spinta green, abbiamo assistito di fatto a un dimezzamento delle raffinerie e sono rimasti pochi grandi poli, controllati da gruppi italiani e internazionali, mentre altri impianti sono stati chiusi, trasformati in depositi oppure riconvertiti alla produzione di biocarburanti. Sulla scena, i protagonisti sono Eni, Ludoil, Saras, Ip, Sonatrach, Q8, Iplom e Alma Petroli.

Il principale polo italiano è quello di Priolo, in Sicilia. La raffineria Isab, con una capacità nell’ordine dei 19 milioni di tonnellate l’anno, rappresenta da sola quasi un quarto della capacità nazionale. Dopo la recente cessione, è oggi controllata da Ludoil, che ha annunciato un importante programma di investimenti per rilanciare il sito. Il piano industriale da 1,3 miliardi si sviluppa in due direzioni. La prima garantisce piena efficienza alle infrastrutture della raffineria, con la rimessa in servizio e l’ammodernamento di alcune unità di processo dismesse. La seconda direzione è la conversione ai biocarburanti. C’è poi Sarroch, in Sardegna, la grande raffineria Sarlux del gruppo Saras, con una capacità di circa 15 milioni di tonnellate l’anno. In Sicilia troviamo Milazzo, oltre 10 milioni di tonnellate di capacità, partecipata al 50% da Eni e al 50% da Kuwait Petroleum Italia, e Augusta, circa 8 milioni di tonnellate, controllata dalla algerina Sonatrach.

Nel Nord Italia il sistema ruota soprattutto attorno a Sannazzaro de’ Burgondi, di Eni, e a Trecate, controllata da Italiana Petroli dopo l’ingresso di Socar. Sannazzaro vale circa 10 milioni di tonnellate di capacità, Trecate circa 9 milioni. A queste si aggiunge Falconara, nelle Marche, anch’essa del gruppo Ip, con una capacità vicina ai 4 milioni di tonnellate. Completano il quadro la raffineria Iplom di Busalla, in Liguria, e Alma Petroli a Ravenna, impianto più piccolo e fortemente specializzato nella produzione di bitumi.

È dunque un sistema concentrato in pochi grandi operatori e non esiste più la frammentazione industriale di un tempo. E proprio per questo ogni fermata, ogni manutenzione straordinaria e ogni decisione di investimento possono avere un peso maggiore sul sistema nazionale.

Ma c’è un altro cambiamento da considerare. Alcune raffinerie non esistono più nella loro forma tradizionale. Venezia e Gela sono state convertite da Eni in bioraffinerie. Livorno è in fase di riconversione. Altri vecchi siti sono diventati depositi e piattaforme logistiche. È la trasformazione della raffinazione italiana: meno petrolio in alcuni impianti, più biocarburanti e nuove produzioni energetiche.

Un passaggio importante, ma con il quale l’Italia deve fare i conti: nel 2025 il consumo nazionale di prodotti petroliferi è stato vicino ai 56 milioni di tonnellate. Il solo gasolio vale circa 26 milioni di tonnellate, la benzina quasi 9 milioni e il carburante per l’aviazione oltre 5 milioni. Numeri che spiegano perché la raffinazione continui a essere strategica anche mentre procede la transizione energetica.

L’Italia dispone, sulla carta, di una capacità di raffinazione superiore ai consumi interni. Ma questo non significa essere autosufficienti: nel 2025 abbiamo importato circa 16 milioni di tonnellate di prodotti raffinati e, contemporaneamente, ne abbiamo esportate oltre 25 milioni. Non è una contraddizione. Il mercato è fatto di prodotti petroliferi diversi e di contratti.

Ma i conti devono tornare. Ecco perché il vertice dell’8 ottobre convocato dai ministri dell’Ambiente, Gilberto Pichetto Fratin e delle Imprese Adolfo Urso, punterà non soltanto a capire quanta capacità di raffinazione abbiamo, ma soprattutto quanta capacità realmente disponibile possiamo mettere in campo, con quali prodotti e in quali tempi.

Quel 23% circa di capacità non utilizzata non è automaticamente una riserva pronta a entrare sul mercato. Bisogna capire raffineria per raffineria quali impianti possono aumentare i volumi, quali unità hanno bisogno di manutenzione, quali sono i limiti logistici, quale greggio è disponibile e quale mix di benzina, gasolio e jet fuel può essere effettivamente prodotto. Non solo, si dovrà ragionare anche sulla quota di export per verificare se, in parte, può essere riportata nei confini nazionali.

Sulla raffinazione e sul fronte petrolifero, «abbiamo una condizione di sofferta sufficienza» e «bisogna settorializzare: forse sul jet fuel dobbiamo stare più attenti mentre sul petrolio e sulla benzina siamo invece in grado di produrcelo», ha detto il ministro dell’Ambiente.

Secondo i dati Unem, in Europa ci sono 77 raffinerie. Anche nel Vecchio Continente si è registrata una progressiva riduzione della capacità, avendo perso circa il 20% degli impianti (circa 35-40 raffinerie) dal 2009 a oggi, con una capacità attuale di circa 12,8 milioni di barili al giorno. Meglio dell’Italia è posizionata solo la Germania (con 15 raffinerie), bene anche la Spagna (9). È quindi ipotizzabile che il governo verificherà se esportiamo in questi Paesi i nostri prodotti invitando eventualmente le società a una gestione diversa della produzione.

Con i petrolieri «si tratta di fare un punto nazionale, ma anche un punto delle relazioni con l’Unione Europea, perché comunque le nostre raffinerie esportano anche», ha detto il ministro Pichetto.

La sfida dell’8 ottobre, si concentrerà poi sul jet fuel: ne consumiamo circa 5 milioni di tonnellate e ne produciamo in questo momento meno di 3. In questo ambito una mano potrebbe arrivare dalle bioraffinerie. Attraverso la produzione di Saf (Sustainable Aviation Fuel), ovvero il cherosene sostenibile per aerei, le bioraffinerie rappresentano una leva strategica per la sicurezza energetica e la continuità del trasporto aereo.

I Saf possono infatti essere miscelati con il jet fuel tradizionale fino al 50% e non richiedono alcuna modifica ai motori degli aeromobili o alle infrastrutture di stoccaggio e distribuzione degli aeroporti. Entrano qui in gioco le bioraffinerie moderne (come quelle di Eni a Gela e Porto Marghera) che permettono di generare combustibile direttamente sul territorio nazionale. L’impianto Enilive di Gela, ad esempio, è già in grado di coprire una quota significativa della domanda europea di Saf.

L’Italia si colloca tra i principali leader europei nella trasformazione industriale verso le bioenergie, posizionandosi stabilmente al quarto posto in Europa per volume complessivo di biocarburanti prodotti. Porto Marghera (Venezia), avviata nel 2014, è stata la prima raffineria tradizionale al mondo a essere interamente convertita in bioraffineria.

Un’ottima scommessa per il futuro. Secondo gli ultimi studi presentati da Teha ed Eni, lo sviluppo della filiera europea dei biocarburanti può valere fino a 66 miliardi di euro in valore aggiunto entro i prossimi decenni. L’Hvo e il Saf sono considerati vettori industriali pronti ed efficienti poiché utilizzano le infrastrutture logistiche e i motori diesel già esistenti, permettendo – per esempio – di decarbonizzare la flotta circolante senza imporre una rottamazione forzata immediata dei veicoli.

authors: Núria Sala Ventura, Albert Cadanet Vilà, Xavier Grau del Cerro, Agustí Sala, Núria Ferragutcasas, Raquel Villanueva, Catalina Serra, Jordi Nopca, JAROMIR CHALABALA

text:
The war in Iran has pushed the price of oil upwards, a fact that has especially affected hydrocarbons. A liter of gasoline costs about 0.4 euros more today than in February, and in many Catalan gas stations it exceeds 2 euros per liter. This means that filling a standard 55-liter tank is about 20 euros more expensive than seven months ago.

Of this amount, nearly half are taxes. In Spain, the price includes the special tax on hydrocarbons —with a temporarily reduced rate— and VAT.

What happens with kerosene for aviation? As a petroleum derivative, this fuel has become significantly more expensive since the outbreak of the conflict in the Persian Gulf in March. According to the European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation (Eurocontrol), the price of fuel for aircraft this month of September has been 4.63 dollars per gallon (1.06 euros per liter), "more than double" the levels of January and February of this year.

But the tax level is completely different: kerosene supplied for international commercial flights and for most flights within the EU is exempt from levies.

Post-war aid

The origin of this exemption dates back to the 1940s, when Europe was just emerging from World War II. In this context of reconstruction, 52 states signed an aviation treaty that would lay the foundations for this precedent. It agreed that the fuel already carried in an aircraft's tank upon landing in another country would be exempt from certain customs duties. Later on, the recommendations of bodies such as the International Air Transport Association and the International Civil Aviation Organization, the United Nations specialized agency for aviation, along with various bilateral agreements signed between states, ended up extending the tax exemption on fuel for international flights.

This regime was consolidated in 2003 in the European Energy Taxation Directive, which establishes that commercial aviation remains exempt from general fuel taxes. Private leisure aviation, however, does have to pay taxes. The directive, however, leaves a window for states that wish to do so to tax fuel for domestic flights and for, if two states decide it bilaterally, them to be able to apply taxes to fuel for flights connecting their territories.

Environmental organizations such as Greenpeace, T&E, or Ecologistas en Acción consider that this legal loophole demonstrates that applying levies is a matter of political will. T&E calculates that this tax exemption is equivalent to an indirect subsidy of more than 30 billion euros per year for EU airlines, which is to the detriment of more sustainable modes of transport such as the train, which does pay taxes on the electricity it consumes. "It is a significant subsidy for fossil fuels that makes flying artificially cheap, shifts environmental costs to the public, and disadvantages cleaner alternatives like the railway," argues Wouter Lemm, representative of Greenpeace in the Netherlands, to ARA.

Airlines, however, are not exempt from taxes. They pay airport fees and in some countries there are taxes on tickets. The sector's employers' associations argue that another tax, in this case on kerosene, in Europe would not reduce consumption, but rather would cause planes to fill their tanks outside the EU.

Javier Gándara, president of the Association of Airlines (ALA, the Spanish employers' association for the sector), recently argued that taxing aviation fuel "does not decarbonize and has a very harmful impact on connectivity and the economy". In his view, this would cause planes to carry more fuel than necessary to save on taxes and would increase CO₂ emissions.

Veto by tourist countries

The increasingly shared consensus that we are living through a climate crisis has translated into various legislative proposals in the EU to revise sector levies. Ursula von der Leyen's European executive promoted a reform in 2021 to introduce a mandatory minimum tax in the EU on kerosene for intra-European commercial flights. However, the veto from the most tourist-oriented states such as Spain, Greece, or Portugal blocked the measure. The Danish presidency of the EU proposed postponing any tax on kerosene until 2035.

As an alternative, Brussels established in 2023 the progressive withdrawal of free carbon dioxide (CO₂) emission allowances, which forced companies to pay for what they emit on flights within the EU. Likewise, last year a regulation came into force that requires suppliers to incorporate a proportion of sustainable aviation fuel: it is currently 2% and must reach 70% by 2050.

Since taxing fuel directly is complex at an international scale, various countries (such as France, Germany, or the Netherlands) have opted to apply "eco-taxes" directly on the passenger ticket, which can be used to finance rail transport.

Regarding these mechanisms, Lemm believes that they can address "a small part of the climate impact of aviation," but argues that "they do not compensate for the absence of an adequate tax on kerosene." "Maintaining this exemption until 2035 would be a climate failure," because "it would prevent investing this money in affordable public transport, railways, and support for vulnerable households," he concludes.

text:
An SNP MSP has called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to reveal when he will spend £200 million promised to an industrial cluster in the Falkirk area.

Local MSP Martyn Day claimed that "not a penny" of £200 million earmarked to support industry at the Grangemouth site has been spent.

It comes as chemical manufacturer Syngenta revealed on Thursday it is considering ceasing all operations in the area, placing 377 jobs at risk.

The company said that while no final decision has been made, it had now entered in formal consultation with trade unions and employees at the site.

It follows a year after more than 400 workers lost their jobs as the Grangemouth oil refinery, Scotland's last, closed.

READ MORE:

Company given £2million funding to protect Grangemouth jobs plans closure

Andy Burnham urged to 'walk the walk' on Grangemouth

SNP demands Grangemouth plan after Burnham's Sustainable Aviation Fuel pledge

Mr Day said: "Firstly, my thoughts are with all the workers of Syngenta and their families at this hugely challenging time.

"The SNP is clear that we firmly oppose the industrial closures at Grangemouth and we will continue to push bosses to reconsider this decision.

"The workers of Grangemouth and surrounding areas have once again been betrayed by this UK Labour Government – the same Labour Government that has spent billions saving industrial jobs in England, but stood back and did nothing when Ineos and Mossmorran went under – we cannot have a repeat of that at Syngenta.

"Labour promised £200 million of support for industry in Grangemouth, but not a penny of it has been delivered."

He added: "Grangemouth needs that money and it needs it now – Andy Burnham must immediately tell the people of Grangemouth exactly when that money is coming and exactly how it will be spent.

"People in Grangemouth and across Scotland are fed-up with being treated as an afterthought by Westminster.

"It is only with the fresh start of independence that we can build a stronger and wealthier country, where Scotland's industry will always be the priority."

text:
Mexico’s Federal Civil Aviation Agency (AFAC) has temporarily grounded two aircraft, XA-GJC and XA-ALV, operated by AirLink, an air ambulance provider, and suspended its maintenance workshop following an inspection. AirLink’s remaining 11 aircraft continue to operate.

AFAC’s findings

AirLink said AFAC found gaps in the recording of maintenance work, specifically pilot reports entered in one aircraft log. AFAC also raised concerns about activity within the company’s maintenance workshop.

The operator said the issues do not affect its air operator certificate (AOC) and that the rest of its fleet continues to be in operation.

CEO of AirLink, Jaime Díaz, said that required maintenance has been carried out and the company was providing documentation to AFAC. In a statement, he said:

“We take the findings seriously, and our job now is to correct every item and provide the corresponding evidence to the authority. We are responding to every inspection comment, and [we expect] the two aircraft will return to service when AFAC confirms they meet all requirements.”

AFAC did not specify the exact issues identified during the inspection.

AirLink’s plan moving forward

AirLink has established an action plan through its safety management system to address the issues moving forward. The plan outlines responsibilities and deadlines assigned to each item identified during the inspection.

The two aircraft will remain grounded until AFAC confirms that all outstanding requirements have been met. The company’s maintenance workshop will remain suspended until its findings have been fully resolved.

You’ve found a good flight deal, picked your dates and are ready to pay — until you get to the baggage allowance. Suddenly, that cheap airfare comes with another bill just to check in a suitcase.

And flying out of Singapore is already getting more expensive, with higher airport charges and a new sustainable aviation fuel levy adding to the cost of air travel.

What "free luggage" credit card perks mean

Banks know that travel perks can be a pretty effective way to get you to sign up for a new card. But when a card advertises "free luggage", that doesn't necessarily mean you're getting free baggage every time you fly.

In Singapore, these perks generally fall into 3 categories:

Physical suitcase sign-up gifts: A one-off welcome gift, usually a suitcase, that you receive after meeting a minimum spending requirement within your first month or two.

Extra checked baggage allowance: An ongoing perk found mainly on airline co-branded cards, giving you additional baggage allowance on eligible flights. This can be handy if you're the type to arrive at the airport hoping your suitcase weighs just under the limit.

Travel insurance with baggage coverage: Some cards include travel insurance when you pay for your trip with the card. This can cover things such as delayed or lost baggage, subject to the policy's terms, limits and exclusions.

There's also one important thing to keep in mind: don't take a suitcase's advertised "retail value" at face value. A $300 suitcase may sound like a fantastic freebie, but luggage brands frequently run sales and promotions, so the actual value may be considerably lower.

That doesn't mean a free suitcase isn't worth taking. If your current luggage has a wheel that's held together by sheer determination, getting a new one as part of a card sign-up can be genuinely useful. Likewise, an extra few kilos of baggage allowance can save you from paying an unpleasant fee at the airport.

The key is to look at the total value of the perk, including the spending required to unlock it, annual fees and any restrictions on when you can use it.

The trick is not to spend more just to hit the target. Instead, time your application around a big purchase you were already planning—whether that's booking flights, buying a laptop or paying for a holiday.

Annual fees add up

text:
EasyJet holidays chief executive Garry Wilson has called on Andy Burnham’s government to “put your money where your mouth is” and back the travel industry through supportive policies.

The prime minister is seeking to prevent airlines from charging parents to sit beside children under 14.

Wilson said such “low-level gestures” should be backed up with more robust measures to help travel businesses.

“When the government gestures on low-level things that will get soundbites to consumers, that’s fine if behind the scenes they’re structurally thinking about how they can support the industry,” he said.

He claimed the government’s approach to the travel sector can appear to be “one step forward and two steps back”.

He called on Labour to “attack” air passenger duty (APD) and speed up the production of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF).

“I think on SAF they need to do a lot more, a lot quicker,” he said, before calling for a rethink on APD.

“You can’t say, ‘We know how important a holiday is’ and then tax the hell out of it. It’s either important or it’s not. They need to put their money where their mouth is,” he added, describing APD as the biggest barrier to growth.

Wilson said easyJet holidays has seen a dramatic shift in booking patterns this year, spurred on by the Middle East conflict and the fuel crisis.

“Twenty percent of our sales are for departures in the next 30 days, which is unheard of,” he said.

He called on the industry to find ways to encourage clients to book earlier, returning to previous trends.

“It’s not good for the industry to have it [the booking window] so late, so we all collectively need to think of initiatives and how we move forward,” he said.

Wilson was speaking at Barrhead Travel’s annual conference in northern Italy.

title: Duurzaam vliegen: CO2-arme reisvluchten? - Clickx magazine
description:
Vliegtuigen vliegen bovendien nog niet op 100 procent SAF.
Het project werd in 2017 stopgezet, zoals met wel meer initiatieven rond elektrisch vliegen.
Die generator zorgt tijdens de kruisvlucht voor de stroomvoorziening, terwijl de batterijen vooral tijdens het opstijgen en landen worden ingezet.
Airbus stelde later dat hybride vliegen de CO2-uitstoot met slechts 5 procent zou terugdringen, best een teleurstelling.
Eerder ontwikkelde het bedrijf al de X1, waarmee de basis voor de ES-30 werd gelegd.
text:
Dat er bij het vliegen massa’s brandstof wordt verbruikt, is je waarschijnlijk wel bekend. Voor een vlucht van Brussels Airport naar Barcelona, die ongeveer twee uur duurt, rekent MyClimate op een CO2-uitstoot van bijna 300 kg per stoel. Vlieg je naar het populaire Malaga, dan mag je daar bijna 60 kg bij optellen, voor een totaal van 353 kg. Een retourvlucht komt daarmee al uit op ongeveer 700 kg CO2-uitstoot. Dat is ongeveer een tiende van de gemiddelde jaarlijkse uitstoot van een inwoner van België. Vermenigvuldig dat met het aantal passagiers in een vliegtuig en je krijgt een behoorlijk indrukwekkend cijfer. Het is dan ook niet zo gek dat de luchtvaart streng wordt aangekeken op haar klimaatimpact. Wereldwijd is de sector verantwoordelijk voor zo’n 2,5 procent van de CO2-uitstoot. Voor wie denkt dat de luchtvaart daarom binnenkort volledig duurzaam wordt, is er slecht nieuws. Er wordt wel degelijk geïnnoveerd, maar voorlopig is het groene karakter van de sector soms vooral terug te vinden in de marketing.

SAF is toch duurzaam?

In de luchtvaartbranche wordt overigens wel degelijk gewerkt aan duurzamere oplossingen. Op technologisch vlak kijkt men bijvoorbeeld naar synthetische en andere alternatieve brandstoffen, ook wel Sustainable Aviation Fuel of SAF genoemd. Sommige maatschappijen vliegen er vandaag al mee en pakken daar tijdens het boeken van een vlucht graag mee uit. Wat daarbij soms minder prominent wordt vermeld, is dat SAF vandaag nog maar op beperkte schaal beschikbaar is en vaak wordt geproduceerd uit grondstoffen zoals gebruikte frituurolie. Vliegtuigen vliegen bovendien nog niet op 100 procent SAF. De Lufthansa Group, waar Brussels Airlines onder valt, gebruikte in 2024 bijvoorbeeld 20.000 ton SAF. Dat was slechts 0,2 procent van de totale brandstofvraag van de groep.

Wereldwijd is het aandeel al even klein. In 2024 was 0,3 procent van alle beschikbare vliegtuigbrandstof SAF, goed voor zo’n 1 miljoen ton. En dan is er nog een ander probleem: SAF is niet volledig emissievrij. Bij de verbranding komt, net als bij kerosine, CO2 vrij. Het idee is dat de koolstof die daarbij vrijkomt eerder uit de atmosfeer is gehaald, bijvoorbeeld via de grondstoffen die voor de brandstof worden gebruikt. Daardoor ligt de totale klimaatimpact over de volledige levenscyclus lager dan bij fossiele kerosine. SAF is daarmee een stap in de goede richting, maar niet de magische oplossing die nodig is.

Batterijen zijn te zwaar

Net als bij auto’s wordt ook bij vliegtuigen gekeken naar batterijen om energie op te slaan en elektromotoren aan te drijven. Alleen botsen vliegtuigbouwers daarbij op een probleem waar elektrische auto’s veel minder last van hebben: gewicht. Airbus’ E-Fan 1.1 was een van de vroege experimenten met elektrisch vliegen. In 2015 vloog het toestel zelfs van het Engelse Lydd naar de Franse kuststad Calais. Het project werd in 2017 stopgezet, zoals met wel meer initiatieven rond elektrisch vliegen. De reden daarvoor is in grote lijnen steeds dezelfde: batterijen zijn zwaar en vliegtuigen hebben enorm veel vermogen nodig om van de grond te komen. Bij kleine vliegtuigen, zoals sommige Cessna’s, is volledig elektrisch vliegen vandaag al mogelijk.

De stap naar een toestel ter grootte van een Boeing 737-800 is echter van een compleet andere orde. Om zo’n vliegtuig voldoende energie mee te geven, zijn enorme batterijpacks nodig. Die voegen zoveel gewicht toe dat het voordeel grotendeels verdwijnt. Bovendien is het bereik met de huidige batterijtechnologie simpelweg te beperkt voor commerciële vluchten over langere afstanden. Wie benieuwd is naar de huidige stand van zaken, vindt op Wikipedia een lijst met elektrische vliegtuigen die in ontwikkeling zijn. Die lijst maakt meteen duidelijk hoe moeilijk de technologie is: er staan heel wat projecten tussen die inmiddels zijn geannuleerd of stilgelegd. Betekent dat dat elektrisch vliegen volledig van tafel is? Ja en nee.

Waar ingenieurs de recente jaren steeds meer naar kijken, is een hybride-opstelling. Net zoals bij auto’s hoeft niet meteen alles volledig elektrisch te zijn. Een deel van de aandrijving kan elektrisch gebeuren, terwijl een andere energiebron voor de rest zorgt. Een voorbeeld daarvan vinden we bij Electra, een spin-off van het Amerikaanse MIT. Het bedrijf begon met het idee voor een vliegtuig dat van kortere landingsbanen kan opstijgen en tegelijk meer bereik en vermogen heeft dan een volledig elektrisch toestel. De EL2, zoals het eerste toestel van Electra heet, is een tweezitter met elektrische motoren, batterijen en een generator. Die generator zorgt tijdens de kruisvlucht voor de stroomvoorziening, terwijl de batterijen vooral tijdens het opstijgen en landen worden ingezet. Dat heeft een belangrijk voordeel. Omdat de elektromotoren niet dezelfde piekbelasting moeten leveren voor het opstijgen, kunnen ze kleiner en efficiënter worden ontworpen dan een conventionele vliegtuigmotor die daar wel rekening mee moet houden.

Electra was zeker niet het enige bedrijf dat met dit idee experimenteerde. Ook Airbus onderzocht hybride vliegen, onder meer met de BAe 146, een vliegtuig met ongeveer 117 zitplaatsen. Het project kreeg de naam E-Fan X en werd ook in de praktijk getest. De aanpak was daarbij ambitieus: een van de vier motoren werd vervangen door een elektrische variant. Daarmee wilde Airbus onderzoeken of elektrische aandrijving uiteindelijk ook op grotere schaal kon worden ingezet. Lang heeft het project echter niet bestaan. Tijdens de coronacrisis werd E-Fan X stopgezet. Airbus stelde later dat hybride vliegen de CO2-uitstoot met slechts 5 procent zou terugdringen, best een teleurstelling. Toch betekent dat niet dat hybride vliegen dood en begraven is.

Kleinere vliegtuigen als eerste stap

Met name de Zweedse fabrikant Heart Aerospace trekt de aandacht met zijn hybride Heart ES-30. Dat toestel moet volledig elektrisch ongeveer 200 kilometer kunnen vliegen. In hybride modus zou het bereik oplopen tot 800 kilometer. Dat maakt het concept interessant voor korte vluchten. Een toestel als de ES-30 zou bijvoorbeeld kleinere vliegtuigen kunnen vervangen die vandaag Europese steden met elkaar verbinden. Er is wel een belangrijke beperking: de ES-30 biedt plaats aan zo’n 30 passagiers. Om het geadverteerde bereik te halen, zou iedere passagier bovendien maximaal 25 kilogram bagage mogen meenemen. Vliegen doet de ES-30 vandaag nog niet. Het hybride toestel moet naar verwachting in 2028 voor het eerst testvluchten uitvoeren, met een geplande indiensttreding vanaf 2031. Air Canada heeft al orders geplaatst voor 30 toestellen, met aanvullende orders van maatschappijen als United en Mesa. Eerder ontwikkelde het bedrijf al de X1, waarmee de basis voor de ES-30 werd gelegd. De X1 heeft ook al testvluchten uitgevoerd. Die bleken zelfs opvallend goedkoop: een testvlucht van 27 minuten zou het bedrijf ongeveer 5 euro aan elektriciteit hebben gekost. Voor korte afstanden kan elektrisch en hybride vliegen dus interessant worden. Maar wie denkt dat we binnenkort elektrisch van Brussel naar New York vliegen, komt bedrogen uit.

Rol weggelegd voor waterstof?

De grootste uitdaging bij elektrisch vliegen blijft het gewicht. Zelfs met solidstatebatterijen, die op termijn voordelen kunnen bieden op het vlak van energiedichtheid en brandveiligheid, blijft de hoeveelheid energie die nodig is om een groot vliegtuig in de lucht te houden een uitdaging. Daar komt nog iets bij: laadtijd en infrastructuur. Stel je voor dat niet alleen elektrische auto’s, maar ook tientallen vliegtuigen op een luchthaven als Schiphol of Brussels Airport tegelijkertijd enorme hoeveelheden elektriciteit moeten kunnen opnemen. Daarvoor is een flinke uitbreiding van de nu al overbezette energie-infrastructuur nodig. Voor grotere toestellen wordt daarom nadrukkelijk gekeken naar waterstof. Uiteindelijk vlieg je daarmee ook op een vorm van elektriciteit, maar fungeert waterstof als energiedrager. Voor auto’s en vrachtwagens is waterstof de voorbije jaren grotendeels naar de achtergrond verdwenen omdat batterijen daarvoor doorgaans efficiënter zijn.

In de luchtvaart ligt dat anders. Het lagere gewicht van waterstof per hoeveelheid opgeslagen energie maakt het concept interessant voor toepassingen waar batterijen te zwaar worden. Er wordt dan ook volop geëxperimenteerd. EasyJet voltooide begin 2026 bijvoorbeeld een test met een vliegtuigmotor die volledig op waterstof draait. Een aangepaste Rolls-Royce Pearl-motor werd tijdens de test naar take-offsnelheden opgevoerd zonder dat daarbij problemen opdoken. Volgens EasyJet toont deze test aan dat moderne vliegtuigmotoren veilig met gasvormige waterstof kunnen werken gedurende een gesimuleerde, volledige vluchtcyclus, inclusief opstarten, opstijgen, kruisvlucht en landing.

Dat klinkt veelbelovend, maar ook hier is een flinke kanttekening nodig. De test werd namelijk uitgevoerd met een motor die je in de wereld van privéjets voorkomt. Het gaat dus niet om de grotere motoren die je bijvoorbeeld op vliegtuigen uit de Boeing 737- of Airbus A320-familie vindt. Voor een echte doorbraak moet bovendien ook de vliegtuigindustrie zelf mee. Airbus kondigde eerder al aan dat zijn ZEROe-project zich onder meer richt op fuel cell-technologie, waarmee waterstof omgezet wordt in elektriciteit. Op de conceptbeelden van Airbus gaat het om vliegtuigen die qua formaat in de buurt komen van toestellen als de A220 en A319. Boeing onderzoekt ondertussen dan weer de mogelijkheden van SAF die met behulp van waterstof kan worden geproduceerd.

Daarmee komen we meteen bij een laatste probleem: waar halen we al die waterstof vandaan? Waterstof komt op aarde weliswaar in enorme hoeveelheden voor, maar niet in de vorm waarin we het rechtstreeks als brandstof kunnen gebruiken. Het moet eerst worden geproduceerd, en dat kost energie. De manier waarop die energie wordt opgewekt, bepaalt vervolgens voor een groot deel hoe duurzaam de waterstof daadwerkelijk is. Zo bestaat er groene waterstof, die met behulp van duurzame elektriciteit wordt geproduceerd, en blauwe waterstof, waarbij aardgas als grondstof wordt gebruikt en een groot deel van de vrijgekomen CO2 wordt afgevangen. Tegelijkertijd biedt waterstof een interessante mogelijkheid voor de luchtvaart. Zodra de technologie voldoende ontwikkeld is, zou een luchthaven in theorie een deel van zijn eigen waterstof kunnen produceren met lokale groene energie. Klinkt veelbelovend. Maar tussen een veelbelovend concept en een vliegtuig dat op grote schaal passagiers vervoert, zit nog een flinke kloof.

title: Feasibility Study on the Integration of a Carbon Capture Device into a Solid Oxide Fuel Cell ...
description: Due to the current and projected increasing demand for air transport, climate-neutrality of aviation until 2050 is a central goal of the European ‘Green Deal’, thus including reduction of carbon dioxide as well as non-carbon dioxide emissions. Using fuel cells, especially solid oxide fuel cells, for energy conversion within aviation propulsion systems is considered a promising solution to reduce carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions. In comparison to other fuel cells suitable for aviation, solid oxide fuel cells exhibit the advantage of a high fuel flexibility. Therefore, they can be operated with sustainable aviation fuel or natural gas instead of hydrogen. This is a significant advantage as the use of sustainable aviation fuel would necessitate fewer modifications and changes to the fuel infrastructure and the tank system of the aircraft. Nevertheless, a main disadvantage of using sustainable aviation fuel is the residual carbon dioxide emissions. Therefore, in this study, the possibility of integrating a carbon capture device into a reference propulsion system is being explored. The optimal location for integration of the capturing device is derived based on the increase of system complexity, the potential energy demand for the capturing process and the capture rate. Furthermore, the chemical reactions along the process chain are modelled, including fuel conversion in an autothermal reforming device, at the solid oxide fuel cell and in a downstream combustion chamber. Consequently, the mass flows of substances, especially sustainable aviation fuel and carbon dioxide, are being obtained based on a reference mission profile. Finally, an estimation of feasible carbon capture rates is conducted derived from the mass and volume of carbon dioxide produced throughout the mission.
text: Due to the current and projected increasing demand for air transport, climate-neutrality of aviation until 2050 is a central goal of the European ‘Green Deal’, thus including reduction of carbon dioxide as well as non-carbon dioxide emissions. Using fuel cells, especially solid oxide fuel cells, for energy conversion within aviation propulsion systems is considered a promising solution to reduce carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions. In comparison to other fuel cells suitable for aviation, solid oxide fuel cells exhibit the advantage of a high fuel flexibility. Therefore, they can be operated with sustainable aviation fuel or natural gas instead of hydrogen. This is a significant advantage as the use of sustainable aviation fuel would necessitate fewer modifications and changes to the fuel infrastructure and the tank system of the aircraft.
