title: Germany Challenges ATR's Turboprop Monopoly: D328eco Assembly Line Launches
description:
In 2019, SNC formed Deutsche Aircraft — initially called Deutsche Regional Aircraft GmbH — specifically to develop an updated variant for commercial production.
At full output, it is designed to produce up to 48 D328eco aircraft per year.
Deutsche Aircraft partnered with Weerts Group, an industrial construction specialist, to develop the site; Deutsche Aircraft holds full financial responsibility for it.
What Comes Before Any Passenger Boards Between the Leipzig FAL inauguration and a passenger stepping onto a D328eco, Deutsche Aircraft still has to thread the certification needle.
Deutsche Aircraft has disclosed Letters of Intent from Private Wings, a German charter operator, for five aircraft, along with additional undisclosed LOIs.
text:
Germany has formally reopened its doors to original regional aircraft production for the first time in more than two decades — and the aircraft industry now has its first credible Western challenger to ATR's de facto monopoly on new turboprop deliveries above 40 seats.

On September 29, Deutsche Aircraft inaugurated its Final Assembly Line (FAL) at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Saxony, marking the moment that a €100 million (approximately $112 million USD) investment in factory infrastructure, flight testing, and supply-chain development translated into a production-ready facility on German soil. It is the first CS25-certified regional aircraft assembly line to open in Germany since Fairchild Dornier ceased production of the original Dornier 328 turboprop in 2002 — a gap of 24 years.

The significance runs beyond a single factory opening. When De Havilland Canada halted production of the Dash 8-400 in 2022, ATR became the only Western manufacturer capable of delivering new turboprops in the 40-plus-seat class. The D328eco, Deutsche Aircraft's 40-seat turboprop built on the DNA of the Dornier 328, is the first aircraft with a credible path to commercial service that changes that calculation.

A Turboprop Reborn With New Technology

The D328eco is not a clean-sheet aircraft. Its airframe descends from the original Dornier 328, which first flew in 1991 and became a workhorse of short-haul European and North American regional aviation before production ended following Fairchild Dornier's 2002 insolvency. 328 Support Services GmbH, the type-certificate holder, was acquired by Sierra Nevada Corporation (SNC) in February 2015. In 2019, SNC formed Deutsche Aircraft — initially called Deutsche Regional Aircraft GmbH — specifically to develop an updated variant for commercial production.

What emerged is a recognizable platform with a substantially upgraded interior. The fuselage has been stretched by approximately 2 meters (6.6 ft) compared to the original 328-100 to accommodate 40 passengers in a 2+1, three-abreast cabin layout. That configuration gives the D328eco a meaningful comfort edge over ATR's 2+2 four-abreast seating on comparable routes.

Under the engine cowlings sit a pair of Pratt & Whitney Canada PW127XT-S turboprops — a customized variant of the PW127 family, which has accumulated more than 208 million flying hours across all variants. The "XT" designation stands for eXTended life: the engine incorporates a redesigned compressor and combustor that delivers a 3% improvement in fuel burn per flight cycle compared to the PW127E/M engines it succeeds. Critically, the PW127XT-S is engineered for full compatibility with 100% Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), including Power-to-Liquid synthetic fuel derived from atmospheric CO2 and renewable electricity — a compliance pathway that matters increasingly as EU SAF-blending mandates tighten.

The cockpit has been fully overhauled. Deutsche Aircraft has selected Garmin's G5000 Prime, announced in June 2025 as the company's most advanced integrated flight deck for Part 25 transport-category aircraft, making the D328eco its first application in this category. The G5000 Prime features multi-core processors, gigabit system connectivity, touchscreen Primary Display Units that are edge-to-edge and sunlight-readable, and Secondary Display Units with 40% more screen area than prior-generation Garmin touch controllers. Integrated autothrottles, an emergency descent mode, and an emergency return capability are standard. Both pilots can interact with the flight deck simultaneously — the system accepts up to 10 simultaneous touchscreen inputs.

What the Leipzig Factory Actually Does

The FAL sits on a 60,500-square-meter (651,000 sq ft / about 15 acres) site at Leipzig/Halle Airport, roughly the footprint of eight football fields. At full output, it is designed to produce up to 48 D328eco aircraft per year. Between 250 and 350 permanent, skilled manufacturing jobs are expected to materialize as the program scales from development into serial production.

Construction proceeded through a groundbreaking ceremony in May 2023, a cornerstone ceremony in April 2025, and a Richtfest (topping-out ceremony) in November 2025. Deutsche Aircraft partnered with Weerts Group, an industrial construction specialist, to develop the site; Deutsche Aircraft holds full financial responsibility for it.

The facility has been designed from the ground up around Industry 4.0 principles: augmented-reality assembly guidance for technicians, battery-powered tooling throughout, automated and driverless logistics systems, paperless production processes, and a target of carbon-neutral operations. Unusually for an OEM facility, customers will be able to observe their individual aircraft being assembled in real time — a level of production transparency that serves both as marketing and as an early-warning mechanism for delivery disputes.

While Leipzig handles final assembly, flight testing, and customer deliveries, Deutsche Aircraft's existing headquarters at the Air Tech Campus in Oberpfaffenhofen, Bavaria, remains home to engineering and EASA certification activities. The TAC 1 test aircraft — Deutsche Aircraft's first D328eco prototype — rolled out at Oberpfaffenhofen in May 2025; a legacy D328 airframe has been flying as a dedicated landing gear testbed since August 5, 2026, while TAC 1 itself continues ground preparations ahead of its own maiden flight.

What Comes Before Any Passenger Boards

Between the Leipzig FAL inauguration and a passenger stepping onto a D328eco, Deutsche Aircraft still has to thread the certification needle.

The company targets type certification under both EASA CS25 and FAA Part 25 rules before the end of 2027, with entry into service in Q4 2027. That dual-certification path is non-negotiable commercially: without FAA Part 25 approval, no US carrier — including charter operators and regional airlines in Canada or India that use American operating frameworks — can put the aircraft in revenue service.

The certification campaign is well underway. On September 8, Deutsche Aircraft confirmed a key milestone in its landing gear program: the landing gear flight tests passed, including Low-Speed Taxi (LST), High-Speed Taxi (HST), and the initial phase of flight testing using a legacy D328 airframe as a dedicated flying testbed. As of the announcement, the test aircraft had accumulated more than 15 hours of ground and flight testing with the new landing gear system. Deutsche Aircraft also changed landing gear suppliers during development and acquired full intellectual property rights for the new system — a move that improves parts availability and supply-chain resilience but added complexity to the test campaign.

What makes the timeline tight is not the certification ambition itself but its compression. If entry into service is truly Q4 2027, that leaves fewer than 15 months from when the landing gear flight testing began in August 2026 to full dual-certification — a schedule that would require an unusually smooth test campaign for a new aircraft type. Deutsche Aircraft has already revised its target once, from an original 2025 entry-into-service goal to the current 2027 target, attributing the slip to stricter regulatory requirements and a program review.

What Is Different About the D328eco vs. the ATR 42

The D328eco enters a market where ATR — the Franco-Italian joint venture between Airbus and Leonardo — has been the sole source of new Western-built turboprops in the 40-plus-seat class since 2022. ATR entered 2026 with a backlog of more than 160 aircraft and recorded 60 gross orders during 2025 alone, including a landmark 40-aircraft firm order from India's FLY91 for the ATR 72-600 placed in September 2026. ATR's leadership has described new market entrants as operating in a "niche" of its broader range.

The technical distinctions between the two aircraft are real. The PW127XT-S engines on the D328eco deliver 3% better fuel burn than the PW127E/M models in older ATR aircraft; ATR's own PW127XT-equipped current-production aircraft also achieve this improvement. The D328eco's 3-abreast cabin gives passengers a seat width similar to narrow-body jets. And the G5000 Prime avionics represent a leap beyond any cockpit currently offered on ATR production aircraft.

What the D328eco does not yet have is a substantial commercial order book. Deutsche Aircraft has disclosed Letters of Intent from Private Wings, a German charter operator, for five aircraft, along with additional undisclosed LOIs. Letters of intent are not firm orders. Markets that Deutsche Aircraft has identified as primary targets — Canada, India, and operators seeking to replace aging Saab 340s and early Dash 8-100s — represent genuine demand, but converting market interest into binding commitments requires an operating aircraft, not a factory.

How the D328eco Gets Built

The supply chain is largely secured. Deutsche Aircraft says more than 95% of supplier contracts are in place. Pratt & Whitney Canada delivers the PW127XT-S engines; Garmin supplies the G5000 Prime avionics; Spanish aerospace manufacturer Aernnova produces the composite empennage, horizontal and vertical stabilizers, and metallic tail cone; Dynamatic Technologies in Bangalore manufactures the rear fuselage; HEGGEMANN AG provides the new landing gear system. Flight data recorders are supplied by Acron Aviation, which signed a long-term supply agreement with Deutsche Aircraft in July 2026.

The aircraft's multi-role variants — the D328 MR (Multi-Role) platform targeting special missions, medevac, and military applications — provide Deutsche Aircraft with a sales channel separate from the commercial airline market. The US Air Force is among the world's largest operators of legacy Dornier 328 aircraft, suggesting a potential upgrade path that would diversify Deutsche Aircraft's customer base beyond commercial operators.

What the Saxony Milestone Means Beyond Airplanes

For Germany, the Leipzig FAL is something more than a production facility. It is the first time in more than two decades that an aircraft carrying a CS25 type certificate has been assembled on German soil — and the first time in more than 60 years that a final assembly line for aircraft has been built in the eastern German states, specifically in Saxony.

The Saxon state government contributed approximately €3.2 million (approximately $3.6 million USD) to the project through the Federal-State GRW program; the Free State of Saxony cited the facility as a complement to existing aerospace research institutions and supplier companies in the region. Federal government support came in the form of backing through Germany's national aerospace policy, with the German government's aerospace coordinator having described Deutsche Aircraft as "a strategic partner for the sustainable development of the aviation industry."

The question that the next 15 months will answer is whether the program that opened its factory doors last week can also deliver an aircraft that passes regulators' scrutiny — and whether the airlines that have expressed interest in the D328eco are willing to convert that interest into purchase agreements once a certified aircraft exists to buy.

Currency conversions in this article are based on exchange rates at the time of publication and are approximate.

Frequently Asked Questions

What makes the D328eco different from its predecessor, the Dornier 328?

The D328eco is a modernized evolution, not a replacement. The fuselage is stretched by about 2 meters (6.6 ft) to seat 40 passengers rather than the original 32-33. The engines are new Pratt & Whitney Canada PW127XT-S turboprops that deliver 3% better fuel burn than earlier variants and are designed for 100% SAF compatibility. The cockpit is entirely new, built around Garmin's G5000 Prime avionics suite — the first installation of this system in a transport-category aircraft — replacing the older glass cockpit of the original 328. The fuselage and wing structure retain the certified aerodynamic baseline, which speeds development compared to a clean-sheet design.

Why does Germany need its own regional aircraft manufacturer?

Germany does not strictly need one, but the reopening of a national production line has strategic and economic dimensions. Regional turboprops serve thin routes that larger jets cannot operate economically — connecting secondary cities and remote communities to hub airports. Germany's aerospace industry had been entirely dependent on Airbus for original civil aircraft production, with no domestically assembled airliner since the Dornier 328 line closed. Beyond national prestige, the facility creates 250 to 350 skilled engineering and manufacturing jobs in Saxony, a region that historically has had fewer high-technology industrial anchors than western Germany. The German government has backed the project through both direct funding and policy statements.

What is the D328eco's biggest competitive challenge before it enters service?

Certification speed. Deutsche Aircraft is targeting both EASA CS25 and FAA Part 25 type certification by late 2027, with first deliveries in Q4 2027. That leaves fewer than 15 months of flying tests — for both the primary test aircraft and the ongoing landing gear campaign — before the company needs a certified aircraft to hand to customers. The company has already moved its target date once, from 2025 to 2027. If the 2027 certification campaign encounters unexpected test findings, which are common in new aircraft programs, the timeline could slip again. The compressed schedule, combined with a commercial order book that still consists largely of Letters of Intent rather than firm orders, means the transition from "factory open" to "aircraft in revenue service" is the critical risk phase of this program.

How does the D328eco fit into sustainable aviation trends?

The PW127XT-S engine is engineered for full compatibility with 100% Sustainable Aviation Fuel, including Power-to-Liquid SAF produced from CO2 and renewable electricity. This positions the D328eco ahead of EU mandates that require increasing SAF blending percentages in aviation fuel sold at European airports, starting at 2% in 2025 and rising over subsequent years. The Leipzig assembly line is itself designed to be carbon-neutral in operation, using battery-powered tooling, renewable energy sources, and paperless processes. Longer term, Deutsche Aircraft has indicated interest in a hydrogen-powered variant of the D328 platform. For now, the practical sustainability case rests on the turboprop's inherent structural advantage: at routes below roughly 500 km (311 miles), turboprops burn significantly less fuel per passenger than regional jets covering the same distance.

text:
The role of Chief Procurement Officer is changing and three leading executives claim procurement has fundamentally shifted from a cost-cutting function to a key part of business strategy.

Procurement LIVE hosted its CPO Strategy Summit in London on September 9, exploring the priorities shaping procurement today and the strategies defining its future.

The panel brought together Graham Scott, Chief Procurement Officer at Jabil, Andrew Swift FCIPS, Chief Procurement Officer at British Council and Ben Terry, Group Chief Procurement Officer at evoke.

The three discussed how the CPO role is changing, navigating geopolitical volatility and AI’s role in the profession.

Omnea Agentic OS Cuts Procurement Cycle Times

With its Agentic Operating System (aOS) for procurement, Omnea is looking to give enterprise teams and AI agents one place to manage suppliers across intake, sourcing, contracting, third-party risk management (TPRM) and supplier management. The aOS is built on a Context Engine, with a library of pre-configured agents running on top and the customer's controls around both.

The aOS is Omnea's answer to two generations of tooling: the heavy, inflexible procure-to-pay (P2P) suites enterprises have leaned on since the early 2000s, and the newer intake and orchestration layers bolted on top that already look out of date.

Ben Freeman, CEO and co-founder of Omnea, says: “Legacy P2P is dying, and orchestration alone is not enough.

“The last wave of intake platforms made procurement faster but not smarter, and some that launched only four years ago already feel like legacy technology. The system that comes next has to build context and improve itself with every approval, rejection and negotiation, rather than automate busywork with bots.

“Our agents run on leading AI models, but that’s not what makes them special. What makes them different is what they know about how your organisation actually buys.”

AI & Regulation: Navigating Procurement’s New Era

This year is shaping up to be the one in which procurement teams must operationalise several major regimes at once, including the EU AI Act, alongside the EU Data Act and CSDDD.

With all this landing on procurement functions at the same time, legal frameworks must become dynamic and adaptable as innovations in technology accelerate.

“The enactment of strict legal safeguards must be weighed against organisationally acceptable risk tolerance thresholds to execute business at speed,” says Shaz Khan, CEO and Co-Founder of Vroozi.

“The next five years of innovation will bring a new wave of technology acceleration, from manufacturing processes to autonomous vehicles. Legal departments will be a partner with purchasing and finance to ensure balance and compromise is met in a fast-paced and unpredictable environment.”

Daniel Coe: Transforming Coca-Cola’s Procurement Strategy

FedEx is helping to power sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) procurement with the use of new agreements projected to secure more than 20 million gallons of neat SAF across five US airports throughout the calendar year of 2027.

This agreement will work across FedEx operations at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), Oakland International Airport (OAK), Miami International Airport (MIA), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW).

The agreements are expected to deliver SAF at blend ratios ranging from 30% to 50%, depending on location.

FedEx is working towards its goal of sourcing 30% of jet fuel from blended alternative sources by 2030, while expanding the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) across its US air network.

"The latest agreements represent an expansion of SAF within the FedEx air network enabled, in part, by state and federal level incentives," says Greg Paulus, Vice President of Enterprise Sourcing.

text:
Avantium N.V. (Amsterdam, the Netherlands) announced the completion of the spin-out of its Parana Technology into Parana Materials B.V. (Geleen, the Netherlands). Parana Materials is a new, independent company focused on the development and commercialization of plant-based, high-performance polyesters such as PISA, PISOX and PEIT/PEIF. The Parana Technology portfolio is distinct from Avantium’s FDCA and PEF (branded as releaf®) technology, which remains fully within Avantium. The transaction is part of Avantium’s strategy to focus resources and investments on its core FDCA and PEF business while enabling other promising technologies in its portfolio to pursue independent growth and commercialization pathways.

Parana Technology enables the production, application and recycling of renewable, high-performance polyesters through simpler and more cost-effective synthesis routes using commercially available monomers such as isosorbide, succinic and oxalic acid, and bio-MEG, and production in existing industrial assets. The technology portfolio includes oxalic acid-based PISOX polyesters, which offer attractive sustainability characteristics, including marine degradability and the potential for a carbon-negative footprint, as well as PISA, PEIT and PEIF polyesters, which combine high mechanical and thermal performance with renewable content for packaging, consumer goods and specialty applications. The technology has attracted interest from leading global consumer brands and materials innovators.

As part of the transaction, Avantium has transferred the assets associated with Parana Technology to Parana Materials, including intellectual property, know-how, projects and a dedicated team. Among the founders of Parana Materials is Gert-Jan Gruter, currently Avantium’s chief technology officer and the inventor of the Parana Technology, who will transfer to the new company following completion of the transaction as chief technology officer of Parana Materials. Parana Materials will be led by Willem-Jan Meijer, who has more than a decade of experience in strategy, licensing, business development and the commercialization of sustainable technologies, including senior leadership positions at Avantium and dab.bio. Avantium will retain a minority shareholding in Parana Materials, allowing Avantium to participate in future value creation while maintaining focus on its strategic priorities.

Parana Materials has been established at Brightlands Chemelot Campus in Geleen, the Netherlands, and starts its next phase with dedicated leadership, funding and infrastructure. The company will assume responsibility for the operation of Avantium’s polymerization pilot plant unit under a lease arrangement. This unit will support Parana Materials’ development, scale-up and customer application activities and will be used for third-party tolling, while allowing Avantium to reduce its overall cost base with minimal operational disruption. Avantium will retain ownership of the unit and continue to have access to its polymerization capabilities through Parana in support of its FDCA and PEF technology.

To support its next phase of development and commercialization, Parana Materials has secured backing from LIOF Participatiefonds (Maastricht, the Netherlands), Limburg’s regional development agency, as well as from its founders. The company has also been awarded support through the Just Transition Fund (JTF) and the Demonstration Energy and Climate Innovation (DEI+) programs. Together, these commitments provide a strong foundation for advancing Parana Materials toward commercial applications and further scale-up of its renewable polyester platform.

Gert-Jan Gruter, chief technology officer and founder of Parana Materials, said: “Parana Materials starts with a clear mission: to turn a distinct portfolio of plant-based polyester technologies into practical solutions for customers. Operating as an independent company gives us the focus and agility to develop PISOX, PISA, PEIT and PEIF together with partners, using production routes designed to fit existing industrial infrastructure. We look forward to building the company and translating customer interest into concrete applications.”

Jeffrey Lutje Spelberg, investment manager of LIOF, added: “Parana Materials combines innovative technology with strong international growth potential. Our investment supports its technical and commercial development while strengthening Limburg’s biobased materials cluster. Its presence at Brightlands Chemelot Campus creates new opportunities for collaboration and innovation, helping build lasting economic value for the region.”

Tom van Aken, chief executive officer of Avantium, said: “The completion of the Parana spin-out is another important step in the execution of our strategy. By creating an independent company with dedicated leadership, funding and development resources, we believe Parana Materials is well positioned to advance its promising polyester technology platform. At the same time, the transaction enables Avantium to sharpen its focus on the commercialization of FDCA and PEF and the execution of our licensing strategy. Through our shareholding in Parana Materials, we retain exposure to the future value creation potential of the technology while allowing the business to pursue its own growth trajectory.”

title: Netherlands Travel Tax and SAF Funding Reset - Travel And Tour World
description:
Netherlands 2027 Flight Tax Is Not a Simple Passenger Tax Cut The most important point for travellers, airlines and travel sellers is that the Netherlands is not reducing air passenger tax across the board.
The Netherlands Tax Administration confirms that transfer passengers are excluded from the tax, alongside flight crew and children under two.
€90 Million SAF Fund Adds a Second Layer to the Aviation Cost Reset Passenger taxation is only one side of the Netherlands’ emerging 2027 aviation policy.
Travel sellers should therefore avoid treating passenger tax as a direct forecast of total ticket-price movements.
Netherlands Is Shifting From One Aviation Price Signal to a More Complex Policy Architecture The Netherlands’ 2027 aviation transition is becoming substantially broader than the flight-tax increase first outlined in 2025.
text:
The Netherlands is entering 2027 with an aviation-cost structure far more complex than a straightforward flight-tax reduction. A distance-based tax will replace the current €30.25 flat rate, while the government is proposing to reduce only the planned long-haul band from €74.81 to €59.43. Medium-haul departures would still rise to €49.87, transfer passengers remain outside the Dutch tax base, and parallel SAF measures are targeting both airline fuel uptake and domestic sustainable-fuel production.

Netherlands 2027 Flight Tax Is Not a Simple Passenger Tax Cut

The most important point for travellers, airlines and travel sellers is that the Netherlands is not reducing air passenger tax across the board.

According to the Dutch government’s official aviation-tax information, passengers departing a Dutch airport currently face a uniform tax of €30.25 in 2026. From 1 January 2027, an already enacted distance-based system introduces separate short-, medium- and long-distance bands.

The government has subsequently proposed changing only the highest band. The long-haul rate had been scheduled to reach €74.81, after indexation, but the Belastingplan 2027 proposes lowering it to €59.43. That amendment still requires parliamentary approval.

This distinction matters because €59.43 remains considerably above the €30.25 charged on every taxable departure in 2026.

The resulting increases against the 2026 flat rate are approximately 2.6 per cent for short-haul, 64.9 per cent for medium-haul and 96.5 per cent for long-haul under the latest proposal. The proposed long-haul amendment nevertheless cuts €15.38, or about 20.6 per cent, from the rate that had otherwise been scheduled for 2027. The underlying official rate figures are published by the Dutch government and Netherlands Enterprise Agency.

Legal Status Is Crucial for 2027 Travel Planning

The distance-based system itself is not merely an aspiration. The Dutch Wet differentiatie vliegbelasting was adopted by both chambers of parliament in December 2025, published on 23 December 2025 and is due to take effect on 1 January 2027.

What remains a proposal as of 3 October 2026 is the new reduction of the indexed long-haul rate from €74.81 to €59.43.

According to the Dutch government’s Belastingplan 2027 information, the new package still requires consideration by the Tweede Kamer and Eerste Kamer. The government expects parliamentary decisions during the remaining 2026 budget process.

Travel businesses should therefore distinguish between the confirmed 2027 distance-based architecture and the still-pending amendment to its highest rate.

The Overlooked Rule Is That Final Destination Determines the Tax

A less visible provision could matter almost as much as the headline rates.

According to the Dutch government, the distance category is determined using the passenger’s final destination, including journeys involving an intermediate connection. The bands are structured around distance from Amsterdam, with European Union destinations and journeys of roughly up to 2,000 kilometres generally falling into the short category, destinations approximately 2,000 to 5,500 kilometres away entering the medium category, and longer journeys entering the highest band.

That means an itinerary starting in the Netherlands does not automatically receive the tax associated with its first flight sector.

The government specifically identifies Egypt and Türkiye as examples of medium-distance destinations and Canada, Mexico, Indonesia and South Africa as long-distance examples. Certain territories, including Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten, Bonaire, Saba and Sint Eustatius, receive the lower rate despite their geographical distance because of their constitutional relationship with the Kingdom of the Netherlands.

The Netherlands Tax Administration confirms that transfer passengers are excluded from the tax, alongside flight crew and children under two.

Transfer Exemption Creates a Different Cost Exposure for Hub Traffic

This is where the 2027 policy becomes particularly significant for aviation economics.

A passenger beginning a taxable long-distance journey in the Netherlands could face the proposed €59.43 tax. A passenger whose international journey merely connects through a Dutch airport remains outside the Dutch passenger-tax base.

That distinction matters because connecting traffic is not marginal to the Dutch aviation system.

According to Schiphol’s official 2025 traffic figures, 68.8 million travellers used the airport during the year. Of these, 43.6 million travelled directly to or from Schiphol, while 25.2 million had a connecting flight. Schiphol directly connected the Netherlands with 301 destinations, including 125 intercontinental points.

During the first half of 2026, another 32.7 million passengers travelled to, from or through Schiphol despite weather disruption and geopolitical pressures on aviation networks.

The scale of connecting traffic makes the transfer exemption commercially important. It means the Dutch tax is structurally more exposed to passengers beginning their journeys in the Netherlands than passengers moving through its principal hub.

Exclusive Analysis: The Real 2027 Divide Is Origin Traffic Versus Connecting Traffic

The most consequential feature of the 2027 system may therefore be less about short-haul versus long-haul flying than about where the passenger begins the journey.

For locally originating passengers, the Netherlands is making distance a stronger determinant of the tax component embedded in the fare. The medium-haul increase is particularly notable because that band receives no new September 2026 relief. Its €49.87 rate is almost €20 above the current flat charge.

Long-haul travellers receive relief only against the previously scheduled 2027 level, not against 2026.

Connecting passengers occupy a different position. Their exemption helps preserve the economics of using the Netherlands as a European transfer hub even as origin passengers become subject to differentiated rates.

This does not establish that passengers will switch airports or airlines. Fare decisions depend on base fares, airport charges, fuel, competition, capacity and network availability. What it does establish is that the statutory tax burden is distributed unevenly across different passenger flows.

For travel managers and tour operators, itinerary structure will therefore become more relevant to interpreting the tax component of Dutch departures.

€90 Million SAF Fund Adds a Second Layer to the Aviation Cost Reset

Passenger taxation is only one side of the Netherlands’ emerging 2027 aviation policy.

According to the Dutch Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, the government has reserved €45 million for a Sustainable Aviation Fuel incentive fund being developed with Schiphol. Schiphol is expected to provide another €45 million, bringing intended funding to €90 million for 2027–2029.

The fund has a very specific design.

Airlines would receive support for SAF blended above the European regulatory obligation, rather than for fuel they are already required to use. The Dutch government contribution remains conditional on European Commission approval.

That distinction prevents the initiative from being confused with a new passenger charge or an automatic airline subsidy.

It is an incentive aimed at additional sustainable-fuel consumption beyond the mandatory baseline.

EU SAF Rules Explain Why Above-Mandate Funding Matters

ReFuelEU Aviation already requires aviation-fuel suppliers at covered EU airports to meet a minimum 2 per cent SAF share from 2025. The mandated share rises to 6 per cent in 2030, with progressively higher requirements thereafter.

The new Dutch-Schiphol fund therefore targets consumption that goes beyond an existing European regulatory floor.

Schiphol identifies cost as one of the main barriers to faster SAF adoption. Its institutional sustainability information states that the fuel is currently almost three times more expensive than conventional kerosene and remains limited in availability. Its previous SAF incentive programme between 2022 and 2024 helped participating airlines use more than 40,000 tonnes.

A Further €300 Million Targets the Supply Side

The 2027 Dutch infrastructure budget reveals another layer that substantially broadens the sustainability story.

According to the official 2027 budget of the Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, €300 million from the Climate and Energy Fund is being invested in the production and scaling of sustainable aviation fuels, including e-SAF and advanced bio-SAF produced through Alcohol-to-Jet technology. The first subsidy decisions are expected in 2027.

This should not automatically be added to the €90 million Schiphol fund and presented as one combined programme because the mechanisms, beneficiaries and budget structures differ.

They can, however, be understood as complementary interventions.

The €90 million initiative primarily targets airline demand above the EU mandate. The €300 million programme targets fuel production and industrial scale-up.

That gives the Netherlands a two-sided SAF strategy entering 2027: stimulate additional consumption while simultaneously attempting to expand the production base.

Why Airlines Face More Than One Cost Signal

Airlines operating in the Netherlands will consequently enter 2027 facing several policy signals at once.

The ticket-tax system increases the passenger-tax component for medium- and long-distance originating journeys. The proposed amendment softens the highest band relative to what had already been scheduled. Transfer traffic remains exempt. Meanwhile, targeted public and airport funding seeks to reduce part of the economic hurdle involved in using more SAF than EU rules require.

Airport charges form another separate cost category.

Schiphol previously established a charging programme under which its airline charges rise substantially over the 2024–2027 period, although the scheduled annual charge movement for 2027 itself is downward compared with 2026. The airport has also been operating a temporary daytime-flight discount through 31 March 2027 in response to exceptional fuel-cost pressures.

Travel sellers should therefore avoid treating passenger tax as a direct forecast of total ticket-price movements.

What Travel Agents and Tour Operators Should Do Before 2027

Separate enacted law from the pending amendment. The distance-based structure is scheduled for 1 January 2027, while the €59.43 long-haul rate still depends on the Belastingplan 2027 legislative process.

Budget medium-haul itineraries carefully. The current proposal leaves the €49.87 medium-distance rate unchanged.

Do not describe €59.43 as a reduction from 2026. It is lower than the previously scheduled 2027 long-haul rate but higher than the current €30.25 charge.

Check final destinations rather than first sectors. Connecting itineraries originating in the Netherlands are categorised according to final destination.

Distinguish transfers from Dutch-origin departures. Genuine transfer passengers remain outside the Dutch air passenger tax.

Avoid guaranteeing fare increases equal to the tax movement. Airlines determine complete fares using multiple commercial and operating inputs.

Do not present the €90 million SAF fund as confirmed passenger funding. It targets airlines blending above the EU mandate and the government contribution requires European Commission approval.

Monitor parliamentary decisions before publishing final 2027 packages. Tax assumptions should be updated once the Belastingplan process is complete.

Netherlands Is Shifting From One Aviation Price Signal to a More Complex Policy Architecture

The Netherlands’ 2027 aviation transition is becoming substantially broader than the flight-tax increase first outlined in 2025.

The country is moving from one uniform passenger levy to three distance-linked rates, proposing relief against the previously scheduled long-haul level, maintaining an exemption that protects transfer traffic, supporting airlines that consume SAF beyond European requirements and preparing major production-side investment in sustainable aviation fuels.

That combination creates different implications for locally originating travellers, transfer passengers, airlines, airports, fuel producers and travel intermediaries.

The central traveller message is therefore precise: 2027 does not bring a general Dutch flight-tax reduction. Medium- and long-distance originating journeys remain substantially more heavily taxed than in 2026 under the current policy path.

The broader industry message is more strategic. The Netherlands is simultaneously attempting to preserve international aviation competitiveness and accelerate aviation decarbonisation by moving some policy support towards targeted fuel incentives rather than relying on passenger taxation alone.

Whether that balance materially changes fares, airline capacity or passenger behaviour cannot yet be established. But from 1 January 2027, the structure governing the cost of departing the Netherlands will become markedly more differentiated than it is today.

text:
Ho Chi Minh City (VNA) - ABB Group of Switzerland has reaffirmed its commitment to supporting Vietnam’s development through advanced electrification and automation technologies, as the country accelerates industrial modernisation, digital transformation and energy transition.

Focus will be placed on energy infrastructure, data centres, talent development and industrial innovation, it said.

The commitment comes as negotiations on a Free Trade Agreement (FTA) between the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) and Vietnam have been concluded. The agreement is expected to strengthen trade, investment and technology cooperation between Vietnam and the four EFTA member states of Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

According to ABB, this marks an important step forward as Vietnam promotes industrial modernisation and energy transition under the Power Development Plan VIII, which is expected to require 136 billion USD in power generation and transmission investments by 2030.

"Vietnam has established itself as one of Asia's most dynamic growth markets, supported by a strong industrial base, a talented workforce, and a growing innovation ecosystem," said Jessica Nguyen, General Director, Country Holding Officer, and Chairwoman of the Board at ABB Vietnam.

"With our Swiss heritage and more than three decades of experience in Vietnam, we are confident that the successful conclusion of the EFTA-Vietnam FTA negotiations will create new opportunities for collaboration, innovation, and investment, while supporting Vietnam's ambitions for industrial modernisation, digitalisation, and sustainable growth."

The group also noted that Vietnam's data centre sector is expanding rapidly, driven by growing demand for cloud computing, AI applications, and digital services. Total data centre power capacity is projected to increase from approximately 580 MW in 2025 to nearly 980 MW by 2030, placing greater emphasis on power reliability, energy efficiency, and sustainability.

This growth comes as Vietnam faces mounting pressure to strengthen its energy infrastructure.

"Data centre are becoming a critical foundation of Vietnam's digital economy. As digital demand accelerates amid growing pressure on the power system, operators need infrastructure that delivers reliability, efficiency, and visibility across their operations. Through ABB's end-to-end portfolio of electrification, automation, and digital energy management solutions, we help customers secure reliable power, optimise energy use, maximise uptime, and advance their sustainability goals. In Vietnam, this expertise is already supporting landmark developments such as CMC Creative Space, one of the country's largest Tier III-standard data centre projects, helping build future-ready facilities that support both business growth and Vietnam's energy transition," said Jessica Nguyen.

Recognising that a skilled workforce is essential to Vietnam's long-term growth and digital transformation, ABB is committed to helping develop the next generation of engineers and technology professionals. Through partnerships with leading institutions including Hanoi University of Science and Technology (HUST), Hanoi University of Industry, RMIT University Vietnam, Ton Duc Thang University, and Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City, ABB helps bridge the gap between academia and industry through knowledge-sharing initiatives, industry training, and access to advanced technologies.

"Vietnamese students possess strong STEM foundations, ambition, and a remarkable willingness to learn and work hard. Yet classroom learning alone is not enough. Future engineers need meaningful exposure to real-world technologies and industry challenges to be job-ready from day one," added Jessica Nguyen. "Through our university partnerships, ABB is helping bridge that gap by equipping the next generation with the practical skills and confidence needed to thrive."

Since establishing operations in Vietnam in 1993, ABB has built a strong nationwide presence and today operates three facilities across the country, including its headquarters in Ho Chi Minh City, an office in Hanoi, and an Electrification Distribution Solutions (ELDS) manufacturing factory in Bac Ninh./.

text:
Hydrogen Utopia secures UK licence to advance waste-to-jet fuel technology

Hydrogen Utopia International PLC (LSE:HUI) has obtained a UK licence from U.S.-based InEnTec Inc. to use its PEM gasification technology in the production of sustainable aviation fuel, expanding the company’s footprint in the waste-to-fuel sector.

The licence, valued at $500,000, allows Hydrogen Utopia to develop and operate systems across the United Kingdom that transform non-recyclable plastics, waste tyres and other discarded materials into syngas suitable for producing sustainable aviation fuel (SAF). The agreement builds on an existing exclusive licence covering the Middle East and North Africa.

The expansion into the UK comes as government policy increasingly supports the development and adoption of lower-carbon aviation fuels. The UK Government is implementing its Low Carbon Fuels Fund alongside a statutory SAF mandate that requires sustainable fuels to account for a progressively larger proportion of aviation fuel demand.

Hydrogen Utopia’s board believes these measures could create a supportive environment for waste-derived fuel projects. The company expects its new licence to improve its prospects of accessing public funding while providing a platform from which it can develop and scale waste-to-SAF infrastructure in the UK.

Despite the potential commercial opportunity, Hydrogen Utopia remains at an early stage financially. The company is pre-revenue, continues to report losses and has generated predominantly negative operating cash flow. Its technical picture is also weak, with the share price trading below important moving averages and the MACD indicator remaining negative.

Traditional valuation measures offer limited support at present because the company is loss-making, resulting in a negative price-to-earnings ratio, while it does not currently provide a dividend yield.

title: Cardano Price Prediction: ADA Stays Below $0.26 Despite Petrobras and the Japan Deal
description:
Cardano (ADA) costs around $0.242 late on Friday evening, October 2, 2026 (according to CoinGecko).

text:
Cardano (ADA) costs around $0.242 late on Friday evening, October 2, 2026 (according to CoinGecko). That puts the price almost exactly on its 200-day moving average, which we calculate at $0.243 from CoinMarketCap daily closes. And it does so in a week with two pieces of news that would have been enough for a price jump at other coins: Brazil's state oil company Petrobras is testing Cardano, and the Cardano Foundation has found a partner in Japan. For the Cardano price prediction what counts, therefore, is why the news has not yet reached the price.

What Petrobras and Pacific Meta have announced

Petrobras has developed two applications on Cardano together with the Ledger Lab of the PUC-Rio university, Cointelegraph reports. The first makes the environmental benefit of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) transferable as a token: an airline or a passenger can acquire the certificate even if the fuel is physically burned somewhere else. A token can be redeemed only once, so that the same certificate is not sold twice. The second application tracks the production, transport and consumption of Diesel R, the group's renewable diesel. Both projects are explicitly at the research stage, and none of those involved names a date for regular operation.

The second report followed on October 1: the Cardano Foundation is working with Pacific Meta, a blockchain incubator from Tokyo that is to help Japanese companies build applications of their own (FXStreet). Japan is no new market for Cardano, where the project has had a large following since its launch in 2017. According to Santiment, the number of daily active addresses almost doubled afterwards to more than 27,500, as CoinCentral quotes it.

Cardano price prediction: the levels on the chart

The one-year chart shows where ADA has come from. A year ago Cardano still cost around $0.85, and the low of the past twelve months sat at roughly $0.14. Over a year the token is down around 72 percent, and over 30 days it is up around 22 percent (CoinGecko).

$0.26 is the level on the upside. On September 25 ADA closed at $0.2586, and the price got no higher than that this autumn. In the 24 hours to Friday evening, that is after the Japan report, the high also reached only around $0.2585. Only a close above it would turn the sideways phase into a breakout.

$0.243, the 200-day moving average, is the line on which ADA is currently balancing. Since September 21, every close has sat between $0.2385 and $0.2586, so within a band of a good eight percent. A price that spent months below this line and is now clinging to it often settles the direction of the coming weeks here.

$0.22 and $0.195 are the levels beneath. The 50-day moving average runs at $0.22, and the lows of August 30 and September 15 sat around $0.195. The recovery that lifted ADA by roughly a third into late September started from there.

Why the news is not carrying the price yet

Both reports are declarations of intent and tests, not revenue. How many transactions the Petrobras project would trigger in operation, and whether any appreciable amount of ADA would be needed for it, cannot be quantified today. For the price, news of that kind is therefore closer to sentiment than to demand. On top of this comes the wider market: Bitcoin moved by just under one percent in the seven days to Friday evening, and without a tailwind from there smaller coins often lack the push.

What is coming up for Cardano in the fourth quarter

The next big step is technical in nature. For the fourth quarter of 2026, according to the roadmap that CoinMarketCap summarises, completion of the first stage of Leios is planned, an extension intended to raise the network's throughput. For November, production operation of the alternative node Amaru has been announced. Dates like these have a record of slipping at Cardano, but they are the next occasions on which it can show whether developers and users come along.

Anyone holding ADA for the long term can delegate the coins in their own wallet to a stake pool. The coins stay in your own custody throughout and remain available at any time; nothing is locked. Anyone who prefers to stake through an exchange should compare terms and custody, for instance in our comparison of staking providers.

Cardano: Your next three steps

First: keep an eye on the closing price, not on the headline. A daily close above $0.26 would be the first sign that the news is reaching the price, and a close below $0.22 the opposite. Second: fit the size of your position to that range, because roughly 18 percent lies between the two levels. Third: with gains, remember the holding period. Coins held for less than a year are taxable on sale in Germany as soon as the annual exemption limit of 1,000 euros is exceeded.

Anyone wondering how the price was read a week ago will find the situation at the time in our Cardano price prediction from September. Crypto assets fluctuate heavily and a total loss is possible. This article places news and price levels in context; it is not a recommendation to buy or sell Cardano.

title: Airlines will spend $4.3 billion on SAF mandates — and nobody has checked the number
description:
IATA estimates airlines will absorb roughly $4.3 billion in SAF compliance costs during 2026, with SAF priced as high as five times conventional jet fuel.
Airlines will spend roughly $4.3 billion on sustainable aviation fuel compliance in 2026, according to IATA.
SAF Certificates SAF Certificates are the documentation UK fuel suppliers use to prove they have met their sustainable aviation fuel obligation.
Main Obligation The Main Obligation is the UK SAF Mandate’s principal SAF requirement, separate from its e-SAF obligation.
IATA estimates roughly $4.3 billion in SAF compliance costs for the 2026 calendar year.
text:
SAF mandates in the EU and UK are adding billions to airline fuel bills, but the numbers come almost entirely from one source. IATA estimates airlines will absorb roughly $4.3 billion in SAF compliance costs during 2026, with SAF priced as high as five times conventional jet fuel.

No independent economic study in the retrieved material confirms that total. The UK and EU also enforce compliance differently — a fixed buyout price per megajoule versus a penalty paired with a duty to supply the shortfall later.

Airlines will spend roughly $4.3 billion on sustainable aviation fuel compliance in 2026, according to IATA. That figure is the spine of the industry’s argument that Europe’s mandates are misfiring.

It is also, on the evidence available, entirely self-reported.

That gap — between a cost everyone cites and a cost nobody outside IATA has checked — is where this story actually lives. The mandates are real. The penalties are written into law. The price of SAF is genuinely higher than jet fuel. What is missing is the mechanism: how a supplier turns a legal obligation into a surcharge, and why the UK and the EU do it in structurally different ways.

Here is what the numbers claim, what the rules require, and what stays unverified.

What IATA’s numbers actually claim

Start with the volume. IATA projects global SAF output in 2026 at about 2.4 million tonnes, a share of roughly 0.8% of all aviation fuel consumed worldwide.

The 2025 comparison is starker. Two million tonnes of SAF, or 0.7% of total fuel requirements, added $4.4 billion to global fuel costs, according to Willie Walsh, IATA’s director general.

Airlines are paying as much as five times the price of conventional jet fuel for SAF under the EU and UK mandates, according to the International Air Transport Association.

Then there is the synthetic subset. Global e-SAF capacity today is just 0.02 million tonnes, against a 2030 mandate target of about 0.6 million tonnes — a gap of roughly thirty times.

Walsh’s verdict is blunt: if the aim was to raise prices and slow progress, the mandates have delivered exactly that. IATA’s stated reason is sequencing. In IATA’s telling, the rules force compliance before the production capacity and market safeguards exist to prevent price gouging.

Two mandates, two penalty machines

The UK and the EU are chasing the same outcome with different instruments, and the difference shapes how cost behaves.

The UK’s SAF Mandate requires suppliers to document eligible fuel with SAF Certificates. A supplier short of certificates can settle the gap at a fixed price per megajoule instead: £0.137 against the Main Obligation, £0.145 against e-SAF.

The EU takes a different route. Under ReFuelEU Aviation, suppliers must place minimum SAF shares on the market at Union airports; fall short and the penalty comes with a duty to deliver the missing fuel in the next reporting period. For synthetic fuel, Article 15 sets up a transitional regime covering 2030–2034 that averages shortfalls and allows them to be supplied later.

Put plainly, the UK lets a supplier buy its way out of a shortfall at a set price. The EU does not: even after a penalty is paid, the missing fuel still has to be delivered.

Source: UK Government, Department for Transport; EUR-Lex, European Union law

Flight deals

Each deal saves 40–80% vs. regular fares:

Why no supplier will show you the surcharge formula

This is the part both sides of the argument skip. No fuel supplier has published a route-level formula for its SAF compliance surcharge — at least, none turned up in the retrieved material.

The obligation sits with suppliers, not airlines. Carriers meet the resulting cost through the fuel price they pay or through contract terms, not through a line item anyone can audit.

That is why “price gouging” stays an accusation rather than a finding. Without a published formula, there is no way to separate a legitimate compliance pass-through from a margin grab.

How a compliance obligation becomes a cost

Under the UK Main Obligation, a supplier that falls short can settle the gap at a legally fixed price per megajoule rather than sourcing more certificates. The e-SAF obligation carries its own buyout, set slightly higher.

This is not a green add-on a passenger chooses at checkout. It is a charge on the obligated supplier, and whether it ever shows up in a fare depends on how fuel contracts and airline pricing are negotiated.

The EU side works the same way in principle. Regulation (EU) 2023/2405 sets the minimum SAF obligations in Article 4 and carries the applicable percentages in Annex I, with the penalty and shortfall machinery in Article 15.

On the UK side, the governing text is the SAF Mandate compliance guidance from the Department for Transport. Neither document, though, yields a single harmonized euro-per-unit penalty.

Reporting by

ATC Intelligence

ATC Intelligence is the research division of Air Traveler Club. Backed by 15 years in Asia-Pacific aviation, we don't just report on the regional market; we live and work in it. By pairing AI-driven data with strict human fact-checking, we provide actionable, trustworthy journalism designed to make your trips to Asia smarter and more affordable.

Follow our daily coverage on Google News, Google Discover, and social media.

Key terms

e-SAF

e-SAF is the synthetic subset of sustainable aviation fuel, governed by its own obligation in both the EU and UK mandates. The EU’s synthetic-fuel rules begin in 2030, and the UK confirms a separate e-SAF obligation alongside its main target. Because the fuel barely exists at commercial scale today, it is the part of the mandate most exposed to supply risk.

SAF Certificates

SAF Certificates are the documentation UK fuel suppliers use to prove they have met their sustainable aviation fuel obligation. A supplier that cannot redeem enough of them may instead settle the shortfall at a fixed buyout price per megajoule. For suppliers, the certificate market — not the buyout — is where the real cost uncertainty sits, since buyout prices are fixed by guidance.

ReFuelEU Aviation

ReFuelEU Aviation is the EU regulation — formally Regulation (EU) 2023/2405 — that sets minimum sustainable aviation fuel shares at Union airports. Article 4 sets the minimum SAF obligations and Annex I carries the applicable percentages, while Article 15 covers penalties, shortfall supply, and the synthetic-fuel transition from 2030 to 2034. Unlike the UK’s fixed buyout, ReFuelEU leaves the size of the penalty to Member States, so the cost of missing the target varies by country.

book-and-claim

Book-and-claim is IATA’s proposed mechanism for letting sustainable aviation fuel bought in one market count toward obligations in another. IATA’s preferred version would operate worldwide alongside harmonized standards, shifting SAF from a local market to a global one. Until a separate standard or registry document exists, airlines cannot treat it as a compliance route — only as a longer-term ambition.

Main Obligation

The Main Obligation is the UK SAF Mandate’s principal SAF requirement, separate from its e-SAF obligation. A supplier that cannot cover it with SAF Certificates may settle at a fixed buyout of £0.137 per megajoule, while the e-SAF obligation is priced at £0.145. That fixed price is the UK’s defining feature: it substitutes cash for certificates, where the EU instead requires the missing fuel to be supplied later.

Questions? Answers.

How much will SAF compliance add to airline fuel bills in 2026?

IATA estimates roughly $4.3 billion in SAF compliance costs for the 2026 calendar year. The comparable 2025 figure was $4.4 billion, drawn from 2 million tonnes of SAF — about 0.7% of total aviation fuel requirements.

What are the UK SAF Mandate buyout prices for a supplier that misses its obligation?

UK compliance guidance sets the buyout at £0.137 per megajoule against the Main Obligation and £0.145 per megajoule against the e-SAF obligation, for suppliers that cannot redeem enough SAF Certificates.

Has anyone independently verified IATA’s $4.3–$4.4 billion SAF cost estimate?

No. No Tier 1 or Tier 2 economic study validating or rejecting that global total was found in the retrieved material, so the figures remain IATA estimates rather than independently verified market data.

How far short is current e-SAF capacity from the 2030 mandate target?

Current global e-SAF capacity sits at about 0.02 million tonnes, while the EU and UK mandates call for roughly 0.6 million tonnes by 2030 — a gap of about thirty times.

What is IATA’s proposed book-and-claim SAF system?

It is IATA’s preferred fix for moving SAF from a local market to a global one: a book-and-claim system operating worldwide alongside harmonized standards. No primary-source operational rulebook for it appears in the supplied evidence.

text:
Each Friday, we publish a round-up of the 20 most important stories on sustainable aviation. You can see previous editions of #Sustainability20 here.

Industry, policy and carbon markets

Canada’s SAF industry faces $32B GDP opportunity as energy security joins climate goals - AviNews

A new analysis estimates that developing Canada’s SAF industry could create a $32 billion GDP opportunity between 2026 and 2040. It presents domestic SAF production as both a decarbonisation opportunity and an energy-security strategy, linking the sector to Canadian feedstocks, jobs and reduced exposure to international fuel-price volatility.

FlyORO joins the ICAO finvest hub as a partner, bringing modular SAF blending expertise to aviation decarbonisation finance - FlyORO

FlyORO has joined ICAO’s Finvest Hub as a partner, contributing modular SAF-blending expertise to the platform’s work on financing aviation-decarbonisation projects. The partnership is aimed at helping projects address the practical infrastructure and financing barriers involved in SAF deployment.

IBA forecasts 87% rise in gross aviation emissions by 2050 despite efficiency gains - GreenAir News

IBA forecasts that global aviation’s gross CO2 emissions could rise by 87% between 2025 and 2050, despite a projected 20% improvement in fleet fuel efficiency. Passenger growth is expected to outpace those efficiency gains, reinforcing the need for measures beyond aircraft efficiency alone.

SimpliFlying’s Carbon Removal Diaries: What really goes into choosing a carbon credit?

After measuring our team’s business travel emissions this summer, we are now examining how to respond to them. This third instalment of our Carbon Removal Diaries explains the questions we asked when evaluating carbon credits, including what a credit represents, how projects are assessed, and what buyers should consider before making a claim.

Sustainable aviation fuels (SAF)

Plug and Arcadia eFuels sign strategic partnership covering more than 1 GW of e-SAF projects, starting with 280 MW to turn danish renewable electricity into jet fuel - GlobeNewswire

Plug Power and Arcadia eFuels have announced a strategic partnership covering more than 1 GW of potential e-SAF projects. The initial 280 MW Danish project is planned to use renewable electricity to produce hydrogen, which would then be combined with captured carbon to make synthetic aviation fuel.

Aether Fuels successfully demonstrates 2.5 barrel-per-day Aurora™ equipment in fully integrated line producing on-spec synthetic aviation fuel - GlobeNewswire

Aether Fuels has demonstrated a fully integrated line producing 2.5 barrels per day of synthetic aviation fuel. The process uses renewable natural gas derived from landfill gas and captured industrial CO2; the company reports that independent testing confirmed the fuel met the FT-SPK specification under ASTM D7566.

ARC Bio demonstrates Canadian forest residue pathway to sustainable aviation fuel - ARC Bio

ARC Bio, a Canadian joint venture between Bioénergie AE Côte-Nord and Alder Renewables, has demonstrated a pilot-scale refinery co-processing pathway for converting forest-industry residues into lower-carbon jet fuel. The approach is intended to use existing refinery infrastructure, although the demonstration does not by itself establish commercial-scale production.

Business, forestry and agriculture leaders unite to advance sustainable aviation fuels - PR Newswire

Agriculture, forestry and business organisations in Georgia, US, have formed a new SAF coalition. Founding members include the Metro Atlanta Chamber, Georgia Forestry Association and Delta Air Lines, working to accelerate domestic biofuel production using Georgia-grown agricultural and forestry feedstocks.

KLM and KLM Cityhopper raise awareness of SAF during The Aviation Challenge - KLM

As part of SkyTeam’s Aviation Challenge, KLM operated a showcase flight from Amsterdam to Delhi on September 28, while KLM Cityhopper flew from Amsterdam to Dublin on September 30 using an Embraer E195-E2. Both flights will test initiatives aimed at improving operational efficiency, reducing fuel consumption and increasing awareness of SAF.

Infrastructure and operational efficiencies

IAG selects SkyBreathe to support fuel efficiency across its airlines - OpenAirlines

IAG will deploy OpenAirlines’ SkyBreathe platform across Aer Lingus, British Airways, Iberia, LEVEL and Vueling, covering more than 600 aircraft. By analysing flight plans, weather and aircraft-performance data, the platform will help identify fuel-saving opportunities and create a common framework for measuring and sharing efficiency initiatives across the group.

Noi Bai International Airport achieves Level 1 Airport Carbon Accreditation - ACI Asia-Pacific

Noi Bai International Airport has achieved Level 1 Airport Carbon Accreditation, becoming the first airport in Vietnam to join the programme. The certification establishes an emissions baseline and provides a foundation for future carbon-reduction measures.

Bristol Airport funds three new projects to cut aviation emissions - ADS Advance

Bristol Airport is funding three technology projects exploring wind power, carbon capture and hydrogen-electric aircraft operations through its 2026 Aviation Carbon Transition Programme. The programme received a record 28 applications and provides up to £150,000 in total funding for projects addressing aviation and airport-related emissions, particularly Scope 3 emissions.

Pittsburgh International Airport deploys robot dogs powered by AI for safety and efficiency - Aerospace Global News

Pittsburgh International Airport is preparing to trial up to four quadruped robots with Pittsburgh-based Skild AI. Initially, they will collect indoor air-quality data and spot issues such as spills and overflowing bins, with later tests covering crowd monitoring, biological-threat detection and terminal deliveries.

New aerodynamic testing technique could improve aircraft efficiency - Aerospace Global News

Pressure-sensitive paint is being used in wind-tunnel testing to capture detailed airflow and surface-pressure data. The technique could help aircraft designers improve aerodynamic efficiency and reduce fuel burn.

Aviation cyber attacks cost organisations $1.4m on average, as phishing and threats to airport operational systems raise concerns - Aerospace Global News

A survey of aviation organisations found that cyber breaches cost an average of $1.4 million. Phishing and attacks on airport operational systems are raising concerns as airports and airlines become increasingly dependent on connected infrastructure.

New technology: Electric and hydrogen

Abu Dhabi plans Emirate-wide air taxi network with over 10 vertiports, targeting late 2026 or early 2027 launch - AviNews

Abu Dhabi is developing an emirate-wide air taxi network with more than 10 vertiports and is targeting passenger operations by late 2026 or early 2027. Archer is expected to supply its Midnight eVTOL aircraft, while Abu Dhabi Aviation will operate the initial service.

Nimbus Aerospace tests quarter-scale prototype in Oregon as hybrid-electric race ramps up - GeekWire

Nimbus Aerospace has conducted test flights of a quarter-scale NX1 prototype in Oregon. The company is developing a proposed six- to eight-seat hybrid-electric aircraft.

Pilotless plane flies over Wichita, putting the future of aviation on display - Yahoo News

Joby Aviation demonstrated an autonomous aircraft over Wichita using a Cessna Caravan retrofitted with its technology. The aircraft used cameras, radar and other sensors to manage flight functions, while a person onboard monitored the demonstration.

Vertical Aerospace opens Valo assembly centre with 1,000 aircraft a year in its sights - Aerospace Global News

Vertical Aerospace has opened its Aircraft Assembly Centre at Cotswold Airport, converting a former Second World War-era and Red Arrows hangar into a production facility for its Valo electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. The first certification-conforming aircraft is scheduled to begin assembly in late 2027, with first flight planned for 2028.

Deutsche Aircraft opens D328eco® final assembly line in Leipzig - Deutsche Aircraft

Deutsche Aircraft has inaugurated the D328eco Final Assembly Line at Leipzig/Halle Airport, marking the programme’s transition from development to serial production. The opening establishes Leipzig as the production site for Germany’s next-generation regional aircraft and marks the return of aircraft manufacturing to Saxony after more than 60 years.

EHang expands global fast-track programme to Vietnam - eVTOL Insights

EHang has expanded its Global Fast Track Program to Vietnam, working with Hanoi’s Department of Science and Technology and local partner HungViet to establish a regulatory sandbox for pilotless eVTOL aircraft. Subject to approval, controlled EH216-S test flights at Hoa Lac Hi-Tech Park will explore unmanned-aircraft traffic management and operations-control systems.

description:
ATLANTA — Agricultural, forestry and business leaders in Georgia have banded together to launch the Georgia Sustainable Aviation Fuel Coalition.
The coalition was established by multiple organizations and businesses, including the Metro Atlanta Chamber, the Georgia Farm Bureau, the Georgia Forestry Association and Delta Air Lines.

text:
ATLANTA — Agricultural, forestry and business leaders in Georgia have banded together to launch the Georgia Sustainable Aviation Fuel Coalition.

The goal is to advance research and the state’s production of biofuels, according to an announcement Wednesday.

The coalition was established by multiple organizations and businesses, including the Metro Atlanta Chamber, the Georgia Farm Bureau, the Georgia Forestry Association and Delta Air Lines.

Sustainable aviation fuel is processed from agricultural and forestry feedstocks to reduce air travel emissions and is designed for compatibility with existing aircraft and fueling infrastructure. Although biofuel currently represents a small share of global aviation fuel, demand is expanding across global markets.

The coalition’s formation builds on the Keep Georgia Forested Act, which Gov. Brian Kemp signed into law in May 2026.

The legislation allows companies to transfer certain tax credits during early construction and operational stages, supporting forestry manufacturing and biofuel production facilities.

Business leaders highlighted the initiative as an opportunity to integrate regional supply chains with aviation demand.

Katie Kirkpatrick, president and CEO of the Metro Atlanta Chamber, outlined the coalition’s goal of coordinating statewide stakeholders.

“This is about aligning Georgia’s natural strengths with real market demand,” Kirkpatrick said.

Agricultural producers said they expect the initiative to expand commercial opportunities for local commodities and the initiative’s connection to Georgia’s farming industry.

The state’s forestry sector, which includes 22 million acres of working forests, is slated to supply additional raw materials for fuel processing.

Prior to the formal launch, coalition members joined the Georgia Research Alliance to secure state funding for an Eminent Scholar focused on forestry research and biofuel development.

Aviation and corporate partners have also signed on to support the project. Boeing, Cox Enterprises and Norfolk Southern are serving as anchor partners, with additional backing from supporting partners RYAM and Gulfstream Aerospace.

Peter Carter, president of Delta Air Lines, pointed to the state’s positioning in the sector as a positive for the new coalition.

“Georgia is well positioned to become a national leader in SAF,” Carter said. “The Georgia SAF Coalition unites organizations committed to advancing that opportunity. Together, we can power the growth of a SAF industry that strengthens Georgia’s economy, supports innovation and creates lasting benefits for communities across the state.”

Federal agriculture officials expressed support for the state-level public-private initiative as well.

The coalition said its immediate priorities include bringing sustainable aviation fuel and biofuel facilities to Georgia, linking university research with industry needs and establishing a supply chain to connect local farms and forests directly to aviation markets.

title: How UCO-Based Biofuels Are Reshaping Aviation and Maritime in the MENA Region
description:
The SAF Opportunity Sustainable Aviation Fuel is chemically similar to conventional jet fuel but produced from renewable feedstocks, including UCO.
The UAE has signalled its commitment through the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Roadmap 2030, which outlines the nation's plan to integrate SAF into its aviation sector.
Maritime Biofuels: Fujairah's Emerging Role Fujairah, already the world's third-largest marine fuelling centre, is positioning itself as a hub for biofuel bunkering.
Why UCO Is the Preferred Feedstock UCO-derived biofuels hold a particular advantage in both aviation and maritime applications.
Every litre of UCO we collect today has the potential to serve road transport, maritime, or aviation applications — depending on market needs and processing pathways.
text:
A New Frontier for Waste-Derived Fuels

When most people think of biodiesel, they picture trucks and buses running on cleaner fuel. But the next chapter of the biofuel story is being written in the skies and on the seas — and the MENA region is emerging as a key player.

Used cooking oil (UCO), the same feedstock that powers road-going biodiesel, is now at the centre of the global push toward Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and cleaner marine fuels. For the UAE and its neighbours, this represents a convergence of environmental ambition, strategic geography, and existing waste-to-fuel infrastructure.

The SAF Opportunity

Sustainable Aviation Fuel is chemically similar to conventional jet fuel but produced from renewable feedstocks, including UCO. When derived from waste oils, SAF can reduce lifecycle carbon emissions by up to 80% compared to fossil jet fuel — without requiring any modifications to aircraft or airport fuelling infrastructure.

The UAE has signalled its commitment through the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Roadmap 2030, which outlines the nation's plan to integrate SAF into its aviation sector. Given that Dubai International Airport is one of the world's busiest aviation hubs and Abu Dhabi continues to expand its aviation footprint, the domestic demand for SAF is substantial and growing.

Notably, MENA Biofuels, a subsidiary of Dubai-headquartered Mercantile and Maritime Group, is currently developing what it describes as the UAE's first commercial SAF production facility in Fujairah. The facility is part of a broader strategy that includes securing sustainable feedstock through international partnerships, such as a recent MoU with Indonesia's Ministry of Cooperatives to develop a nationwide UCO collection ecosystem.

This cross-border collaboration highlights a critical reality: the SAF industry will require feedstock volumes that exceed what any single country can supply domestically, making international UCO supply chains essential.

Maritime Biofuels: Fujairah's Emerging Role

Fujairah, already the world's third-largest marine fuelling centre, is positioning itself as a hub for biofuel bunkering. The maritime sector faces increasing pressure from the EU's FuelEU Maritime regulation, which mandates progressive reductions in greenhouse gas emissions from shipping fuels starting with a 2% reduction against the 2020 baseline.

B24 blends — consisting of 24% UCO methyl ester (UCOME) mixed with very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) — have already entered the Fujairah market, though supply constraints and sporadic demand have limited uptake so far. Industry participants expect demand to accelerate as shipowners prepare for more stringent IMO and EU mandates in the coming years.

The partnership between Uniper Energy Dubai and Neutral Fuels to deliver maritime biofuel in Fujairah is one example of how UAE-based producers are connecting local UCO-to-biodiesel capability with the maritime sector's decarbonisation needs.

Why UCO Is the Preferred Feedstock

UCO-derived biofuels hold a particular advantage in both aviation and maritime applications. Because the feedstock is 100% waste — no virgin crops are used — it avoids the sustainability controversies associated with palm oil or soy-based biofuels. Under EU regulations, waste-derived biofuels receive favourable treatment in emissions accounting and are not subject to the crop-based feedstock caps that limit other biofuel types.

For ISCC-certified producers like Neutral Fuels, this means UCO-derived biodiesel and its derivatives are well-positioned to meet the traceability and sustainability requirements of international markets, including export destinations in Europe.

The MENA Advantage

The MENA region has several structural advantages in the emerging biofuel supply chain. The UAE and GCC states host some of the world's highest per-capita food service activity, generating significant volumes of UCO. Strategic locations like Fujairah provide direct access to major shipping lanes. And established refining infrastructure can be adapted for biofuel production.

Saudi Arabia, through its Vision 2030 programme, has also begun exploring biofuel integration as part of its energy diversification strategy. As cross-border feedstock agreements develop and regulatory frameworks mature, the potential for a MENA-wide biofuel ecosystem becomes increasingly tangible.

What This Means for Neutral Fuels

Neutral Fuels' 14-plus years of UCO collection and biodiesel production experience positions us at the foundation of this expanding value chain. Every litre of UCO we collect today has the potential to serve road transport, maritime, or aviation applications — depending on market needs and processing pathways.

As SAF and marine biofuel demand scales up across the region, the importance of robust, certified UCO collection networks will only grow. For businesses generating used cooking oil, this means your waste stream is becoming more valuable — and more strategically important — than ever before.
